title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: The Division of Labour

The greatest improvements in the productive power of labour, and most of the skill, dexterity, and judgment with which labour is anywhere directed or applied, seem to have resulted from the division of labour. The effects of the division of labour on the general business of society are easiest to understand if we look at how it works in particular manufactures. People commonly suppose it is carried furthest in some very trivial trades—not perhaps because it really is taken further in them than in more important ones, but because, in those small trades meant to supply the minor wants of only a small number of people, the total number of workers must necessarily be small, so that those employed in every branch of the work can often be gathered into the same workshop and placed all at once before the observer's eyes.

In the great manufactures, by contrast—those meant to supply the great wants of the great mass of the people—every branch of the work employs so many workers that it is impossible to gather them all into one workshop. We can rarely see at any one time more than those employed in a single branch. So although in such manufactures the work may actually be divided into far more parts than in the more trivial trades, the division is nowhere near as obvious, and for that reason has been far less noticed.

Let me take an example, then, from a very trivial manufacture, but one in which the division of labour has very often been remarked upon: the trade of the pin-maker. A worker not trained in this business (which the division of labour has turned into a distinct trade), and unfamiliar with the machinery used in it (the invention of which the same division of labour has probably prompted), could scarcely, with his utmost effort, make one pin in a day, and certainly could not make twenty. But in the way this business is now carried on, not only is the whole task a specialized trade, but it is divided into a number of branches, most of which are likewise specialized trades. One man draws out the wire; another straightens it; a third cuts it; a fourth sharpens the point; a fifth grinds the top to receive the head; making the head requires two or three separate operations; fitting it on is its own job; whitening the pins is another; and even packing them into paper is a trade in itself. In this way the important business of making a pin is divided into about eighteen distinct operations, which in some factories are all performed by separate hands, though in others the same man will sometimes perform two or three of them. I have seen a small factory of this kind where only ten men were employed, so that some of them performed two or three distinct operations. Though they were very poor, and therefore only poorly supplied with the necessary machinery, they could, when they put in the effort, make among them about twelve pounds of pins in a day. A pound contains upwards of four thousand pins of a medium size. Those ten people, therefore, could make among them upwards of forty-eight thousand pins in a day. Each person, then, making a tenth of forty-eight thousand pins, may be regarded as making four thousand eight hundred pins a day. But if they had all worked separately and independently, with none of them trained in this particular business, they certainly could not each have made twenty pins a day—perhaps not even one; that is, certainly not the two hundred and fortieth part, and perhaps not the four thousand eight hundredth part, of what they are now able to do as a result of a proper division and combination of their various operations.

In every other art and manufacture the effects of the division of labour are similar to what they are in this very trivial one, though in many of them the labour can neither be subdivided so far nor reduced to such simple operations. The division of labour, however, as far as it can be introduced, brings about in every art a proportionate increase in the productive power of labour. The separation of different trades and occupations from one another seems to have come about because of this advantage. This separation, too, is generally carried furthest in those countries that enjoy the highest degree of industry and improvement: what is the work of one man in a primitive society is generally the work of several in an advanced one. In every advanced society the farmer is generally nothing but a farmer, and the manufacturer nothing but a manufacturer. The labour needed to produce any one finished manufacture, too, is almost always divided among a great many hands. Think how many different trades are employed in each branch of the linen and woollen manufactures, from the growers of the flax and the wool to the bleachers and smoothers of the linen, or to the dyers and dressers of the cloth! The nature of agriculture, it is true, does not allow so many subdivisions of labour, nor so complete a separation of one business from another, as manufactures do. It is impossible to separate the business of the grazier from that of the corn-farmer as completely as the trade of the carpenter is commonly separated from that of the smith. The spinner is almost always a different person from the weaver; but the ploughman, the harrower, the sower of the seed, and the reaper of the corn are often the same. Since the occasions for these different kinds of labour come round with the different seasons of the year, it is impossible for one man to be constantly employed in any one of them. This impossibility of making so complete and entire a separation of all the different branches of labour in agriculture is perhaps the reason why improvement in the productive power of labour in this art does not always keep pace with improvement in manufactures. The most prosperous nations, it is true, generally surpass all their neighbours in agriculture as well as in manufactures; but they are usually more distinguished by their superiority in the latter than in the former. Their lands are in general better cultivated, and—having more labour and expense bestowed upon them—they produce more in proportion to the extent and natural fertility of the ground. But this superiority of produce is seldom much greater than in proportion to the superiority of labour and expense. In agriculture the labour of the rich country is not always much more productive than that of the poor; or at least it is never so much more productive as it commonly is in manufactures. So the corn of the rich country, of the same quality, will not always come to market cheaper than that of the poor country. The corn of Poland, at the same quality, is as cheap as that of France, despite the greater wealth and improvement of France. The corn of France, in its corn-growing provinces, is fully as good and in most years sells at about the same price as the corn of England, even though France is perhaps inferior to England in wealth and improvement. The corn-lands of England, however, are better cultivated than those of France, and the corn-lands of France are said to be much better cultivated than those of Poland. But though the poor country, despite its inferior cultivation, can to some degree rival the rich in the cheapness and quality of its corn, it can claim no such competition in its manufactures—at least if those manufactures suit the soil, climate, and situation of the rich country. The silks of France are better and cheaper than those of England, because the silk manufacture—at least under the present high duties on the importation of raw silk—does not suit the climate of England as well as that of France. But the hardware and the coarse woollens of England are beyond all comparison superior to those of France, and much cheaper too, at the same quality. In Poland there are said to be scarcely any manufactures of any kind, apart from a few of those coarser household manufactures without which no country can well get by.

This great increase in the quantity of work that the same number of people can perform as a result of the division of labour is owing to three distinct circumstances: first, to the increase in dexterity in each particular worker; second, to the saving of the time that is commonly lost in moving from one kind of work to another; and last, to the invention of a great many machines that make labour easier and shorter, and enable one man to do the work of many.

First, the improvement in the worker's dexterity necessarily increases the quantity of work he can perform; and the division of labour, by reducing each man's business to one simple operation and making that operation the sole employment of his life, necessarily increases the worker's dexterity a great deal. A common smith, though used to handling the hammer, who has never been used to making nails, will—if on some particular occasion he is obliged to try—scarcely be able, I am assured, to make above two or three hundred nails in a day, and very bad ones at that. A smith who has been used to making nails, but whose sole or main business has not been that of a nailer, can seldom, with his utmost diligence, make more than eight hundred or a thousand nails in a day. I have seen several boys under twenty years of age who had never practised any other trade than making nails, and who, when they exerted themselves, could each make upwards of two thousand three hundred nails in a day. Yet making a nail is by no means one of the simplest operations. The same person blows the bellows, stirs or mends the fire as needed, heats the iron, and forges every part of the nail; in forging the head, too, he has to change his tools. The various operations into which making a pin or a metal button is subdivided are all of them much simpler, and the dexterity of the person whose sole life's work it has been to perform them is usually much greater. The speed with which some of the operations of those manufactures are performed exceeds what anyone who had never seen them would suppose the human hand capable of acquiring.

Second, the advantage gained by saving the time commonly lost in moving from one sort of work to another is much greater than we might at first imagine. It is impossible to pass very quickly from one kind of work to another that is carried on in a different place and with quite different tools. A country weaver who also cultivates a small farm must lose a good deal of time moving from his loom to the field and from the field back to his loom. When the two trades can be carried on in the same workshop, the loss of time is no doubt much less. Even in that case, however, it is still considerable. A man commonly dawdles a little as he turns his hand from one sort of employment to another. When he first starts the new work he is seldom very keen and energetic; his mind, as they say, is not on it, and for some time he trifles rather than applies himself to good purpose. The habit of dawdling and of slack, careless application, which is naturally—or rather necessarily—acquired by every country worker who is obliged to change his work and his tools every half hour, and to turn his hand in twenty different ways almost every day of his life, makes him almost always sluggish and lazy, and incapable of any vigorous effort even on the most pressing occasions. Quite apart from his lack of dexterity, then, this cause alone must always considerably reduce the quantity of work he is able to perform.

Third and last, everyone must realize how much labour is made easier and shorter by the use of proper machinery. There is no need to give an example. I will only point out, therefore, that the invention of all those machines by which labour is so much eased and shortened seems originally to have been owing to the division of labour. Men are far more likely to discover easier and quicker methods of achieving any object when their whole attention is directed toward that single object than when it is scattered among a great variety of things. But as a result of the division of labour, each man's whole attention naturally comes to be directed toward some one very simple object. It is therefore naturally to be expected that one or another of those employed in each particular branch of labour will soon find out easier and quicker methods of doing his own particular work, whenever the nature of the work allows such improvement. A great many of the machines used in those manufactures in which labour is most subdivided were originally the invention of ordinary workers who, being each employed in some very simple operation, naturally turned their thoughts to finding easier and quicker ways of performing it. Anyone who has often visited such manufactures must frequently have been shown very ingenious machines that were the inventions of such workers, made to ease and speed up their own particular part of the work. In the first fire engines {this was the term then used for steam engines}, a boy was constantly employed to open and shut, by turns, the passage between the boiler and the cylinder, depending on whether the piston rose or fell. One of these boys, who liked to play with his companions, noticed that by tying a string from the handle of the valve that opened this passage to another part of the machine, the valve would open and shut without his help, leaving him free to amuse himself with his playmates. One of the greatest improvements ever made to this machine since it was first invented was, in this way, the discovery of a boy who wanted to save himself some labour.

Not all the improvements in machinery, however, have been the inventions of those who had occasion to use the machines. Many improvements have been made by the ingenuity of the machine-makers, once making them became a specialized trade; and some by those called philosophers, or men of speculation, whose trade is not to do anything but to observe everything, and who on that account are often able to combine the powers of the most distant and dissimilar objects. In the progress of society, philosophy or speculation becomes, like every other employment, the chief or sole trade and occupation of a particular class of citizens. Like every other employment, too, it is subdivided into a great many different branches, each of which provides occupation for its own particular tribe or class of philosophers; and this subdivision of employment in philosophy, as in every other business, improves dexterity and saves time. Each individual becomes more expert in his own particular branch, more work is done on the whole, and the quantity of knowledge is considerably increased by it.

It is the great multiplication of the products of all the different arts, as a result of the division of labour, that brings about, in a well-governed society, that universal prosperity which reaches down to the lowest ranks of the people. Every worker has a great quantity of his own work to dispose of beyond what he himself needs; and since every other worker is in exactly the same situation, he is able to exchange a great quantity of his own goods for a great quantity—or, what comes to the same thing, for the price of a great quantity—of theirs. He supplies them abundantly with what they need, and they supply him just as amply with what he needs, and a general plenty spreads itself through all the different ranks of society.

Look at the way of life of the most ordinary craftsman or day-labourer in a civilized and thriving country, and you will see that the number of people whose industry has gone, even if only in small part, into providing him with it exceeds all reckoning. The woollen coat, for example, that covers the day-labourer, coarse and rough as it may look, is the product of the combined labour of a great many workers. The shepherd, the sorter of the wool, the wool-comber or carder, the dyer, the scribbler, the spinner, the weaver, the fuller, the dresser, with many others, must all combine their different arts to complete even this humble product. How many merchants and carriers, besides, must have been employed in transporting the materials from some of these workers to others who often live in a very distant part of the country? How much commerce and shipping in particular, how many shipbuilders, sailors, sail-makers, and rope-makers, must have been employed to bring together the various dyes used by the dyer, which often come from the remotest corners of the world? What a variety of labour, too, is needed to produce the tools of even the humblest of these workers! To say nothing of such complicated machines as the sailor's ship, the fuller's mill, or even the weaver's loom, let us consider only what a variety of labour is required to make that very simple machine, the shears with which the shepherd clips the wool. The miner, the builder of the furnace for smelting the ore, the feller of the timber, the burner of the charcoal used in the smelting-house, the brickmaker, the bricklayer, the men who tend the furnace, the millwright, the forger, the smith—all of them must combine their different arts to produce these shears. Were we to examine in the same way all the different parts of his dress and household furniture—the coarse linen shirt he wears next to his skin, the shoes that cover his feet, the bed he lies on and all the parts that make it up, the kitchen-grate at which he prepares his food, the coals he uses for that purpose, dug from the bowels of the earth and brought to him perhaps by a long sea and land journey, all the other utensils of his kitchen, all the furniture of his table, the knives and forks, the earthen or pewter plates on which he serves and divides his food, the various hands employed in preparing his bread and his beer, the glass window that lets in the heat and the light while keeping out the wind and the rain, together with all the knowledge and skill needed to make that beautiful and fortunate invention without which these northern parts of the world could scarcely afford a comfortable dwelling, along with the tools of all the different workers employed in producing these various conveniences—if we examine, I say, all these things and consider what a variety of labour goes into each of them, we shall realize that without the help and cooperation of many thousands the very humblest person in a civilized country could not be provided for, even in what we very mistakenly imagine to be the easy and simple way in which he is commonly accommodated. Compared, it is true, with the more extravagant luxury of the great, his accommodation must no doubt seem extremely plain and simple; and yet it may perhaps be true that the accommodation of a European prince does not always exceed that of an industrious and frugal peasant as much as the accommodation of that peasant exceeds that of many an African king, the absolute master of the lives and liberties of ten thousand naked savages.

title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: On the Principle That Gives Rise to the Division of Labour.

The division of labour, which produces so many benefits, was not in the first place the result of any human wisdom that foresaw and aimed at the general prosperity it creates. It is the necessary—though very slow and gradual—consequence of a particular tendency in human nature, a tendency that has no such broad benefit in view: the tendency to trade, barter, and exchange one thing for another.

Whether this tendency is one of those basic principles of human nature for which no further explanation can be given, or whether—as seems more likely—it is the necessary result of our capacities for reason and speech, is not something we need to investigate here. It is shared by all people, and found in no other kind of animal, which appear to know neither this nor any other sort of agreement. Two greyhounds chasing the same hare sometimes look as if they are acting in a kind of coordination. Each turns the hare toward its companion, or tries to cut it off when its companion turns it toward itself. But this is not the result of any agreement; it is simply the accidental coming-together of their desires on the same object at that particular moment. No one has ever seen a dog make a fair and deliberate exchange of one bone for another with another dog. No one has ever seen one animal use its gestures and natural cries to signal to another: this is mine, that is yours; I am willing to give this for that. When an animal wants to get something from a person, or from another animal, it has no other way of persuading them except to win the favour of those whose help it needs. A puppy fawns on its mother, and a spaniel tries by a thousand charms to catch the attention of its master at dinner when it wants to be fed by him. People sometimes use the same tactics with one another, and when they have no other way of getting others to act as they wish, they try by every kind of servile and flattering attention to win their good will. There is not enough time, however, to do this on every occasion. In a civilized society a person constantly needs the cooperation and help of great numbers of people, while a whole lifetime is barely enough to make a few real friends. In almost every other kind of animal, each individual, once it reaches maturity, is entirely independent, and in its natural state needs the help of no other living creature. But a human being has an almost constant need for the help of others, and it is useless to expect that help from their goodwill alone. He is far more likely to succeed if he can engage their self-interest in his favour, and show them that it is to their own advantage to do what he asks of them. Anyone who offers another person a deal of any kind is proposing exactly this. Give me what I want, and you shall have what you want, is the meaning of every such offer; and this is how we obtain from one another the far greater part of the services we need. It is not from the kindness of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their concern for their own interest. We appeal not to their humanity but to their self-love, and we never talk to them about our own needs, but about their advantages. Nobody but a beggar chooses to depend chiefly on the goodwill of his fellow citizens. And even a beggar does not depend on it entirely. The charity of kind-hearted people does, it is true, supply the whole fund of his subsistence. But although this principle ultimately provides him with all the necessities of life he needs, it neither does nor can provide them to him exactly as he needs them, when he needs them. The greater part of his occasional needs are met in the same way as everyone else's—by deal, by barter, and by purchase. With the money one person gives him he buys food. The old clothes another gives him he exchanges for other clothes that suit him better, or for lodging, or for food, or for money, with which he can buy food, clothes, or lodging, as he needs.

Just as it is through dealing, bartering, and buying that we obtain from one another the greater part of the mutual services we need, so it is this same trading disposition that originally gives rise to the division of labour. In a tribe of hunters or shepherds, suppose one particular person makes bows and arrows more quickly and skillfully than anyone else. He often exchanges them with his companions for cattle or venison, and he eventually finds that in this way he can get more cattle and venison than if he went out into the field to catch them himself. Out of regard for his own interest, then, the making of bows and arrows becomes his main occupation, and he becomes a kind of armourer. Another excels at making the frames and coverings of their little huts or movable houses. He gets used to being helpful in this way to his neighbours, who reward him in the same manner with cattle and venison, until at last he finds it in his interest to devote himself entirely to this work and become a kind of house-carpenter. In the same way a third becomes a smith or a brazier; a fourth, a tanner or dresser of hides and skins, which make up the main part of the clothing of primitive peoples. And so the certainty of being able to exchange all that surplus part of the produce of his own labour—the part beyond what he consumes himself—for whatever parts of the produce of other men's labour he may need, encourages every man to take up a particular occupation, and to develop and bring to perfection whatever talent or natural gift he may have for that particular kind of work.

The difference in natural talents between different people is, in reality, much smaller than we suppose; and the very different abilities that seem to set apart men of different professions once they are grown up are, in many cases, not so much the cause as the effect of the division of labour. The difference between the most unlike characters—between a philosopher and an ordinary street porter, for example—seems to arise not so much from nature as from habit, custom, and education. When they came into the world, and for the first six or eight years of their lives, they were perhaps very much alike, and neither their parents nor their playmates could see any notable difference between them. At about that age, or soon after, they come to be employed in very different occupations. The difference in their talents then begins to be noticed, and it gradually widens, until at last the philosopher's vanity is willing to acknowledge scarcely any resemblance at all. But without the disposition to trade, barter, and exchange, every man would have had to obtain for himself every necessity and convenience of life that he wanted. Everyone would have had the same duties to perform and the same work to do, and there could have been no such difference of employment as could by itself give rise to any great difference of talents.

Just as it is this disposition that creates the difference in talents so striking among men of different professions, so it is this same disposition that makes that difference useful. Many tribes of animals, all acknowledged to belong to the same species, are endowed by nature with a far more remarkable difference of character than appears—before custom and education take effect—to exist among people. By nature a philosopher is not half so different in ability and disposition from a street porter as a mastiff is from a greyhound, or a greyhound from a spaniel, or this last from a shepherd's dog. Yet these different kinds of animals, though all of the same species, are of hardly any use to one another. The strength of the mastiff is in no way assisted by the swiftness of the greyhound, or by the keenness of the spaniel, or by the obedience of the shepherd's dog. The effects of these different abilities and talents, for want of the power or the inclination to barter and exchange, cannot be brought together into a common stock, and contribute nothing at all to the better support and convenience of the species. Each animal is still obliged to support and defend itself, separately and independently, and gains no advantage at all from the variety of talents with which nature has distinguished its fellows. Among human beings, by contrast, the most unlike abilities are useful to one another: the different products of their respective talents, through the general disposition to trade, barter, and exchange, are brought, as it were, into a common stock, where every man may buy whatever part of the produce of other men's talents he needs.

title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: That the Division of Labor Is Limited by the Extent of the Market.

Since it is the ability to exchange that creates the opportunity for the division of labor, the extent of that division must always be limited by the extent of that ability to exchange—or, to put it another way, by the size of the market. When the market is very small, no one has any incentive to devote himself entirely to a single occupation, because he lacks the ability to trade the whole surplus of what his own labor produces, beyond what he himself consumes, for the parts of other men's labor that he needs.

There are certain kinds of work, even of the humblest sort, that can only be carried on in a large town. A porter, for instance, can find employment and a living nowhere else. A village is far too narrow a sphere for him; even an ordinary market town is barely large enough to keep him constantly occupied. In the isolated houses and tiny villages scattered across a region as empty as the Scottish Highlands, every farmer has to be his own family's butcher, baker, and brewer. In such places you can hardly expect to find even a smith, a carpenter, or a mason within twenty miles of another in the same trade. The scattered families living eight or ten miles from the nearest such worker must learn to do for themselves a great many small jobs that, in more populous countries, they would call in those tradesmen to do. Country workmen almost everywhere are forced to take on all the different branches of industry that are closely enough related to involve the same kind of materials. A country carpenter handles every sort of work made of wood; a country smith every sort made of iron. The carpenter is not only a carpenter, but a joiner, a cabinetmaker, even a wood-carver, as well as a wheelwright, a plow-wright, and a maker of carts and wagons. The smith's occupations are even more varied. It would be impossible for a trade as specialized as nail-making to exist in the remote, inland parts of the Scottish Highlands. Such a worker, making a thousand nails a day over three hundred working days a year, would produce three hundred thousand nails in a year. But in such a place it would be impossible to sell even a thousand—that is, a single day's work in the whole year. Because water transport opens a wider market to every kind of industry than land transport alone can provide, it is along the seacoast and the banks of navigable rivers that industry of every kind naturally begins to subdivide and improve itself, and often it is only a long time afterward that these improvements spread into the inland parts of the country. A broad-wheeled wagon, manned by two men and drawn by eight horses, carries and brings back nearly four tons of goods between London and Edinburgh in about six weeks. In roughly the same time a ship, crewed by six or eight men and sailing between the ports of London and Leith, frequently carries and brings back two hundred tons of goods. With the help of water transport, then, six or eight men can carry and bring back, in the same time, the same quantity of goods between London and Edinburgh as fifty broad-wheeled wagons manned by a hundred men and drawn by four hundred horses. So for two hundred tons of goods carried by the cheapest land transport from London to Edinburgh, one must charge the upkeep of a hundred men for three weeks, plus both the upkeep and the wear and tear—nearly equal to upkeep—of four hundred horses and fifty large wagons. For the same quantity of goods carried by water, one need charge only the upkeep of six or eight men, the wear and tear of a ship of two hundred tons' burden, and the value of the greater risk, or the difference in insurance between land and water transport. If there were no link between those two places except land transport, then, since no goods could be carried from one to the other except those whose price was very high in proportion to their weight, they could carry on only a small part of the trade that now exists between them, and consequently could give only a small part of the encouragement they now offer each other's industry. There could be little or no trade of any kind between the distant parts of the world. What goods could bear the cost of land transport between London and Calcutta? And even if any were precious enough to support that cost, how safely could they be carried through the territories of so many uncivilized nations? Yet those two cities now carry on a very considerable trade with each other, and by mutually providing a market, give a great deal of encouragement to each other's industry.

Since these are the advantages of water transport, it is natural that the first improvements in skill and industry should appear where this convenience opens the whole world as a market for the produce of every kind of labor, and that they should always be much slower to spread into the inland parts of the country. For a long time the inland regions can have no market for most of their goods except the country that surrounds them and separates them from the seacoast and the great navigable rivers. The extent of the market, therefore, must for a long time be proportional to the wealth and population of that surrounding country, and consequently their improvement must always come after the improvement of that country. In our North American colonies, the plantations have consistently followed either the seacoast or the banks of navigable rivers, and have scarcely anywhere spread any considerable distance from both.

The nations that, according to the most reliable history, appear to have been civilized first were those who lived around the coast of the Mediterranean Sea. That sea, by far the largest inlet known in the world, having no tides and therefore no waves except those raised by the wind alone, was extremely favorable to the world's infant navigation, thanks to the smoothness of its surface, the multitude of its islands, and the closeness of its neighboring shores—at a time when men, ignorant of the compass, were afraid to lose sight of the coast, and when the imperfect art of shipbuilding made them afraid to trust themselves to the rough waves of the open ocean. To pass beyond the Pillars of Hercules—that is, to sail out through the Strait of Gibraltar—was long regarded in the ancient world as a most remarkable and dangerous feat of navigation. It was late before even the Phoenicians and Carthaginians, the most skillful navigators and shipbuilders of those ancient times, attempted it; and for a long time they were the only nations that did.

Of all the countries on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea, Egypt seems to have been the first in which either agriculture or manufacturing was cultivated and improved to any considerable degree. Upper Egypt nowhere extends more than a few miles from the Nile, and in Lower Egypt that great river splits into many different canals, which—with a little help from human effort—seem to have provided a network of water transport not only between all the great towns, but between all the substantial villages, and even to many farmhouses in the countryside, much as the Rhine and the Meuse do in Holland today. The extent and ease of this inland navigation was probably one of the chief causes of Egypt's early development.

The improvements in agriculture and manufacturing likewise seem to have been very ancient in the provinces of Bengal in the East Indies, and in some of the eastern provinces of China, though the full antiquity of this is not confirmed by any histories whose authority we, in this part of the world, are well assured of. In Bengal, the Ganges and several other great rivers form a great many navigable canals, just as the Nile does in Egypt. In the eastern provinces of China, too, several great rivers form a multitude of canals through their different branches, and by connecting with one another provide an inland navigation far more extensive than that of either the Nile or the Ganges, or perhaps than both put together. It is striking that neither the ancient Egyptians, nor the Indians, nor the Chinese encouraged foreign trade, but all seem to have drawn their great wealth from this inland navigation.

All the inland parts of Africa, and all that part of Asia lying any considerable distance north of the Black and Caspian seas—ancient Scythia, modern Tartary and Siberia—seem in every age of the world to have been in the same uncivilized and barbarous state in which we find them today. The Sea of Tartary is the frozen ocean, which permits no navigation; and although some of the greatest rivers in the world run through that country, they are too far apart from one another to carry trade and communication through most of it. Africa has none of those great inlets—such as the Baltic and Adriatic in Europe, the Mediterranean and Black seas in both Europe and Asia, and the gulfs of Arabia, Persia, India, Bengal, and Siam in Asia—to carry maritime trade into the interior of that great continent; and the great rivers of Africa are too far apart from one another to give rise to any considerable inland navigation. Besides, the trade that any nation can carry on by means of a river that does not split into a great number of branches or canals, and that flows into another country before it reaches the sea, can never be very large, because the nations that hold that other territory always have it in their power to block the connection between the upper country and the sea. The navigation of the Danube is of very little use to the various states of Bavaria, Austria, and Hungary, compared with what it would be if any one of them controlled its whole course down to where it falls into the Black Sea.

title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: ON THE ORIGIN AND USE OF MONEY.

Once the division of labour has been thoroughly established, the produce of a man's own labour can supply only a very small part of what he needs. He supplies by far the greater part of his wants by exchanging the surplus of his own labour's produce—whatever is left over beyond his own consumption—for the parts of other men's produce that he happens to need. Every man, then, lives by exchanging, or becomes to some degree a merchant, and the society itself grows into what is properly called a commercial society.

But when the division of labour first began, this power of exchanging must often have been badly clogged and hampered in its workings. Suppose one man has more of a certain commodity than he himself needs, while another has less. The first would naturally be glad to dispose of part of his surplus, and the second to buy it. But if this second man happens to have nothing the first one needs, no exchange can take place between them. The butcher has more meat in his shop than he can possibly eat, and the brewer and the baker would each be willing to buy some of it. But they have nothing to offer in exchange except the various products of their own trades, and the butcher is already supplied with all the bread and beer he immediately needs. In this case no exchange can be made between them. He cannot be their merchant, nor they his customers, and so they are all less useful to one another. To avoid the inconvenience of such situations, every prudent man in every period of society, after the division of labour was first established, must naturally have tried to manage his affairs so as to keep on hand at all times—besides the particular produce of his own work—a certain quantity of some one commodity or other that he imagined few people would refuse in exchange for the produce of their own labour. Many different commodities, it seems likely, were thought of and used for this purpose one after another. In the rough ages of society, cattle are said to have been the common instrument of commerce; and though they must have been a most inconvenient one, in old times things were frequently valued by the number of cattle given in exchange for them. Homer says that the armour of Diomede cost only nine oxen, but that of Glaucus cost a hundred oxen. Salt is said to be the common instrument of commerce and exchange in Abyssinia; a kind of shell in some parts of the coast of India; dried cod in Newfoundland; tobacco in Virginia; sugar in some of our West India colonies; hides or dressed leather in some other countries; and there is to this day a village in Scotland where, I am told, it is not uncommon for a workman to carry nails instead of money to the baker's shop or the alehouse.

In every country, however, men seem at last to have been driven by overwhelming reasons to prefer metals above every other commodity for this purpose. Metals can not only be kept with as little loss as any other commodity—scarcely anything being less perishable than they are—but they can also be divided, without any loss, into any number of parts, and those parts can easily be melted back together again. This is a quality that no other equally durable commodity possesses, and more than any other quality it makes metals fit to be the instruments of commerce and circulation. The man who wanted to buy salt, for example, and had nothing but cattle to give in exchange, would have been forced to buy salt to the value of a whole ox, or a whole sheep, at a time. He could rarely buy less than this, because what he had to give for it could rarely be divided without loss; and if he wished to buy more, then for the same reasons he would have been forced to buy double or triple the quantity—that is, the value of two or three oxen, or of two or three sheep. If, on the other hand, instead of sheep or oxen he had metals to give in exchange, he could easily match the quantity of metal to the precise quantity of the commodity he immediately needed.

Different nations have used different metals for this purpose. Iron was the common instrument of commerce among the ancient Spartans, copper among the ancient Romans, and gold and silver among all rich and commercial nations.

These metals seem originally to have been used for this purpose in rough bars, without any stamp or coinage. Thus Pliny tells us (Pliny, Natural History, book 33, chapter 3), on the authority of Timaeus, an ancient historian, that until the time of Servius Tullius the Romans had no coined money but used unstamped bars of copper to buy whatever they needed. These rough bars, then, served at that time as money.

The use of metals in this rough state involved two very considerable inconveniences: first, the trouble of weighing them, and second, the trouble of assaying them. With the precious metals, where a small difference in quantity makes a great difference in value, even weighing them with proper exactness requires at least very accurate weights and scales. Weighing gold in particular is a delicate operation; with the coarser metals, where a small error would be of little consequence, less accuracy would no doubt be needed. Yet we would find it excessively troublesome if, every time a poor man had occasion to buy or sell a farthing's worth of goods, he was obliged to weigh out the farthing. Assaying is still more difficult and still more tedious, and unless part of the metal is properly melted in the crucible with the right dissolving agents, any conclusion drawn from it is extremely uncertain. Before coined money was instituted, however, unless people went through this tedious and difficult operation, they were always liable to the grossest frauds and cheats; and instead of a pound weight of pure silver or pure copper they might receive, in exchange for their goods, an adulterated mixture of the coarsest and cheapest materials that had nevertheless been made to look like those metals on the surface. To prevent such abuses, to make exchanges easier, and thereby to encourage all sorts of industry and commerce, it has been found necessary, in all countries that have made any considerable progress toward improvement, to stamp a public mark on certain quantities of the particular metals commonly used in those countries to buy goods. This is the origin of coined money and of those public offices called mints—institutions of exactly the same nature as the aulnagers and stamp-masters of woollen and linen cloth. All of them are equally meant to certify, by means of a public stamp, the quantity and uniform quality of these different commodities when they are brought to market.

The first public stamps of this kind affixed to the metals in circulation seem in many cases to have been intended to certify what was both the hardest and the most important thing to certify—namely, the goodness or fineness of the metal. They seem to have resembled the sterling mark now stamped on silver plate and bars, or the Spanish mark sometimes stamped on ingots of gold, which, being struck on only one side of the piece and not covering the whole surface, certifies the fineness but not the weight of the metal. Abraham weighs out to Ephron the four hundred shekels of silver he had agreed to pay for the field of Machpelah. They are said, however, to be the merchant's current money, and yet they are received by weight, not by count, in just the same way that ingots of gold and bars of silver are at present. The revenues of the ancient Saxon kings of England are said to have been paid not in money but in kind—that is, in food and provisions of all sorts. William the Conqueror introduced the custom of paying them in money. This money, however, was for a long time received at the exchequer by weight, not by count.

The inconvenience and difficulty of weighing these metals exactly gave rise to the institution of coins, whose stamp, covering both sides of the piece entirely and sometimes the edges too, was supposed to certify not only the fineness but the weight of the metal. Such coins, therefore, were received by count, as they are now, without the trouble of weighing.

The names of these coins seem originally to have expressed the weight or quantity of metal they contained. In the time of Servius Tullius, who first coined money at Rome, the Roman as, or pondo, contained a Roman pound of good copper. It was divided, like our Troy pound, into twelve ounces, each of which contained a real ounce of good copper. The English pound sterling, in the time of Edward I, contained a pound, Tower weight, of silver of a known fineness. The Tower pound seems to have been somewhat more than the Roman pound and somewhat less than the Troy pound. The Troy pound was not introduced into the mint of England until the eighteenth year of Henry VIII. The French livre, in the time of Charlemagne, contained a pound, Troy weight, of silver of a known fineness. The fair of Troyes in Champagne was at that time attended by all the nations of Europe, and the weights and measures of so famous a market were generally known and respected. The Scots money pound, from the time of Alexander I to that of Robert Bruce, contained a pound of silver of the same weight and fineness as the English pound sterling. English, French, and Scots pennies, too, all originally contained a real pennyweight of silver—the twentieth part of an ounce, and the two-hundred-and-fortieth part of a pound. The shilling, too, seems originally to have been the name of a weight. “When wheat is at twelve shillings the quarter,” says an ancient statute of Henry III, “then the wastel bread of a farthing shall weigh eleven shillings and fourpence.” The proportion, however, between the shilling and either the penny on the one hand or the pound on the other does not seem to have been as constant and uniform as the proportion between the penny and the pound. During the first dynasty of the kings of France, the French sou, or shilling, appears on different occasions to have contained five, twelve, twenty, and forty pennies. Among the ancient Saxons a shilling appears at one time to have contained only five pennies, and it is not unlikely that it was as variable among them as among their neighbours, the ancient Franks. From the time of Charlemagne among the French, and from that of William the Conqueror among the English, the proportion between the pound, the shilling, and the penny seems to have been uniformly the same as it is now, though the value of each has changed greatly; for in every country in the world, I believe, the greed and injustice of princes and sovereign states, abusing the trust of their subjects, have gradually reduced the real quantity of metal originally contained in their coins. In the later ages of the republic, the Roman as was reduced to the twenty-fourth part of its original value, and instead of weighing a pound came to weigh only half an ounce. The English pound and penny at present contain only about a third, the Scots pound and penny about a thirty-sixth, and the French pound and penny about a sixty-sixth part of their original value. By means of these operations, the princes and sovereign states that carried them out were able, in appearance, to pay their debts and meet their obligations with a smaller quantity of silver than would otherwise have been required. It was, however, only in appearance, for their creditors were really cheated out of part of what was owed to them. All other debtors in the state were allowed the same privilege and could repay, with the same nominal sum in the new and debased coin, whatever they had borrowed in the old. Such operations, therefore, have always proved favourable to the debtor and ruinous to the creditor, and have sometimes produced a greater and more widespread revolution in the fortunes of private persons than could have been caused by a very great public disaster.
It is in this way that money has become, in all civilized nations, the universal instrument of commerce, through which goods of every kind are bought and sold, or exchanged for one another.

I shall now go on to examine what rules men naturally follow in exchanging goods either for money or for one another. These rules determine what may be called the relative, or exchangeable, value of goods.

The word VALUE, it should be noted, has two different meanings: sometimes it expresses the usefulness of a particular object, and sometimes the power of buying other goods that possession of that object brings. The first may be called “value in use”; the second, “value in exchange.” The things that have the greatest value in use frequently have little or no value in exchange; and, on the contrary, those that have the greatest value in exchange frequently have little or no value in use. Nothing is more useful than water, but it will buy scarcely anything; scarcely anything can be had in exchange for it. A diamond, on the contrary, has scarcely any value in use, yet a very great quantity of other goods can frequently be had in exchange for it.
In order to investigate the principles that govern the exchangeable value of commodities, I shall try to show:
First, what is the real measure of this exchangeable value; that is, what the real price of all commodities consists of.
Second, what are the different parts of which this real price is composed.

And, lastly, what are the different circumstances that sometimes raise some or all of these different parts of price above their natural or ordinary rate, and sometimes sink them below it; or, in other words, what are the causes that sometimes prevent the market price—that is, the actual price of commodities—from coinciding exactly with what may be called their natural price.

I shall try to explain these three subjects as fully and clearly as I can in the three following chapters, and for this I must very earnestly beg the reader for both patience and attention: his patience, to work through a detailed account that may in some places seem unnecessarily tedious; and his attention, to understand what may, even after the fullest explanation I am able to give, still appear somewhat obscure. I am always willing to risk being tedious in order to be sure I am clear; and even after taking the utmost pains to be clear, some obscurity may still remain on a subject that is by its very nature extremely abstract.

title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: On the Real and Nominal Price of Commodities, or Their Price in Labour and Their Price in Money.

Every person is rich or poor depending on how far he can afford to enjoy the necessities, comforts, and pleasures of human life. But once the division of labour has fully taken hold, a man's own labour can supply him with only a very small part of these things. By far the greater part he has to get from the labour of other people, and he is rich or poor according to the quantity of that labour which he can command, or which he can afford to buy. The value of any commodity, then, to the person who owns it and who does not mean to use or consume it himself but to trade it for other commodities, is equal to the quantity of labour it lets him buy or command. Labour, therefore, is the real measure of the exchangeable value of all commodities.

The real price of anything—what it really costs the man who wants to acquire it—is the toil and trouble of acquiring it. What anything is really worth to the man who has acquired it and wants to dispose of it, or trade it for something else, is the toil and trouble it can spare him and can impose on other people. Whatever is bought with money, or with goods, is paid for by labour just as much as what we get through the exertion of our own bodies. That money, or those goods, do indeed save us this toil. They contain the value of a certain quantity of labour, which we exchange for what is at the time assumed to contain the value of an equal quantity. Labour was the first price, the original purchase money paid for all things. It was not by gold or silver, but by labour, that all the wealth of the world was originally bought; and its value, to those who own it and want to trade it for some new products, is exactly equal to the quantity of labour it can enable them to buy or command.

Wealth, as Mr Hobbes says, is power. But the person who either earns or inherits a great fortune does not necessarily gain or inherit any political power, whether civil or military. His fortune may perhaps give him the means of acquiring both; but merely owning that fortune does not automatically convey either to him. The power that owning it immediately and directly conveys to him is the power to purchase a certain command over all the labour, or over all the produce of labour, that is then in the market. His fortune is greater or smaller exactly in proportion to the extent of this power—that is, to the quantity of other men's labour, or, what amounts to the same thing, of the produce of other men's labour, which it enables him to buy or command. The exchangeable value of everything must always be exactly equal to the extent of the power it conveys to its owner.

But although labour is the real measure of the exchangeable value of all commodities, it is not the measure by which their value is usually estimated. It is often difficult to determine the ratio between two different quantities of labour. The time spent on two different kinds of work will not by itself always settle this ratio. The different degrees of hardship endured, and of skill exercised, must also be taken into account. There may be more labour in an hour of hard work than in two hours of easy business; or in an hour spent practising a trade that took ten years to learn than in a month of effort at an ordinary, undemanding job. But it is not easy to find any accurate measure of either hardship or skill. In trading the various products of different kinds of labour for one another, some allowance is in fact commonly made for both. It is adjusted, however, not by any precise measure, but by the haggling and bargaining of the market, according to that sort of rough equality which, though not exact, is good enough for carrying on the business of everyday life.

Besides, every commodity is more often traded for, and so compared with, other commodities than with labour. It is therefore more natural to estimate its exchangeable value by the quantity of some other commodity than by the quantity of labour it can produce. Most people, too, understand better what is meant by a quantity of a particular commodity than by a quantity of labour. The one is a plain, tangible thing; the other an abstract idea, which, though it can be made clear enough, is not quite so natural and obvious.

But once barter ceases and money becomes the common instrument of trade, every particular commodity is more often traded for money than for any other commodity. The butcher seldom carries his beef or mutton to the baker or the brewer in order to trade them for bread or beer; instead he carries them to the market, where he trades them for money, and afterwards trades that money for bread and beer. The amount of money he gets for them also governs the quantity of bread and beer he can afterwards buy. So it is more natural and obvious for him to estimate their value by the quantity of money—the commodity for which he immediately trades them—than by the quantity of bread and beer, the commodities for which he can trade them only through the go-between of another commodity; and rather to say that his butcher's meat is worth three-pence or four-pence a pound than that it is worth three or four pounds of bread, or three or four quarts of small beer. So it comes about that the exchangeable value of every commodity is more often estimated by the quantity of money than by the quantity of labour or of any other commodity that can be got in exchange for it.

Gold and silver, however, like every other commodity, vary in their value; they are sometimes cheaper and sometimes dearer, sometimes easier and sometimes harder to buy. The quantity of labour that any particular quantity of them can buy or command, or the quantity of other goods it will trade for, always depends on the richness or poverty of the mines that happen to be known around the time such exchanges are made. The discovery of the abundant mines of America reduced, in the sixteenth century, the value of gold and silver in Europe to about a third of what it had been before. Since it took less labour to bring those metals from the mine to the market, so, once brought there, they could buy or command less labour; and this revolution in their value, though perhaps the greatest, is by no means the only one that history records. But just as a measure of quantity—such as the natural foot, fathom, or handful, which is continually varying in its own size—can never be an accurate measure of the quantity of other things, so a commodity that is itself continually varying in its own value can never be an accurate measure of the value of other commodities. Equal quantities of labour may be said, at all times and places, to be of equal value to the labourer. In his ordinary state of health, strength, and spirits, and at his ordinary level of skill and dexterity, he must always lay down the same portion of his ease, his liberty, and his happiness. The price he pays must always be the same, whatever the quantity of goods he gets in return for it. Of these, indeed, it may sometimes buy a greater and sometimes a smaller quantity; but it is the value of the goods that varies, not that of the labour which buys them. At all times and places, that is dear which is hard to come by, or which costs much labour to acquire; and that is cheap which can be had easily, or with very little labour. Labour alone, therefore, never varying in its own value, is alone the ultimate and real standard by which the value of all commodities can at all times and places be estimated and compared. It is their real price; money is only their nominal price.

But although equal quantities of labour are always of equal value to the labourer, yet to the person who employs him they appear sometimes to be of greater and sometimes of smaller value. He buys them sometimes with a greater and sometimes with a smaller quantity of goods, and to him the price of labour seems to vary like that of everything else. It appears dear to him in the one case and cheap in the other. In reality, however, it is the goods that are cheap in the one case and dear in the other.

In this ordinary sense, then, labour, like commodities, may be said to have a real and a nominal price. Its real price may be said to consist in the quantity of the necessities and comforts of life given for it; its nominal price, in the quantity of money. The labourer is rich or poor, well or badly rewarded, in proportion to the real, not the nominal, price of his labour.

The distinction between the real and the nominal price of commodities and labour is not a matter of mere theory, but may sometimes be of considerable practical use. The same real price is always of the same value; but because of the variations in the value of gold and silver, the same nominal price is sometimes of very different values. So when a landed estate is sold subject to a perpetual rent, if it is intended that this rent should always be of the same value, it matters to the family in whose favour it is reserved that it should not be fixed as a particular sum of money. Its value would in that case be liable to variations of two different kinds: first, those arising from the different quantities of gold and silver contained at different times in coin of the same denomination; and second, those arising from the different values of equal quantities of gold and silver at different times.

Princes and sovereign states have frequently imagined that they had a short-term interest in reducing the quantity of pure metal contained in their coins; but they have seldom imagined that they had any interest in increasing it. The quantity of metal contained in the coins of all nations, I believe, has accordingly been almost continually decreasing, and hardly ever increasing. Such variations, therefore, tend almost always to lower the value of a money rent.

The discovery of the mines of America lowered the value of gold and silver in Europe. This decline, it is commonly supposed—though I suspect without any certain proof—is still going on gradually, and is likely to continue for a long time. On that assumption, then, such variations are more likely to lower than to raise the value of a money rent, even if it were stipulated to be paid not in such a quantity of coined money of such a denomination (in so many pounds sterling, for example), but in so many ounces, either of pure silver or of silver of a certain standard.

Rents that have been reserved in corn have kept their value much better than those reserved in money, even where the denomination of the coin has not been altered. By the 18th of Elizabeth it was enacted that a third of the rent of all college leases should be reserved in corn, to be paid either in kind or according to the current prices at the nearest public market. The money arising from this corn rent, though originally only a third of the whole, is, in the present day, according to Dr Blackstone, commonly close to double what arises from the other two-thirds. The old money rents of colleges must, by this account, have sunk to almost a fourth of their ancient value, or are worth little more than a fourth of the corn they were formerly worth. But since the reign of Philip and Mary the denomination of the English coin has undergone little or no alteration, and the same number of pounds, shillings, and pence has contained very nearly the same quantity of pure silver. This decline, therefore, in the value of the money rents of colleges has come entirely from the decline in the price of silver.

When the decline in the value of silver is combined with a reduction in the quantity of it contained in coin of the same denomination, the loss is frequently even greater. In Scotland, where the denomination of the coin has undergone much greater alterations than it ever did in England, and in France, where it has undergone still greater than it ever did in Scotland, some ancient rents, originally of considerable value, have in this way been reduced almost to nothing.

Equal quantities of labour will, at widely separated times, be bought more nearly with equal quantities of corn—the labourer's subsistence—than with equal quantities of gold and silver, or perhaps of any other commodity. Equal quantities of corn, therefore, will at widely separated times be more nearly of the same real value, or enable their owner to buy or command more nearly the same quantity of other people's labour. They will do this, I say, more nearly than equal quantities of almost any other commodity; for even equal quantities of corn will not do it exactly. The labourer's subsistence, or the real price of labour, as I shall try to show later, is very different on different occasions; more generous in a society advancing toward wealth than in one that is standing still, and in one that is standing still than in one that is going backwards. Every other commodity, however, will at any particular time buy a greater or smaller quantity of labour in proportion to the quantity of subsistence it can buy at that time. A rent reserved in corn, therefore, is liable only to the variations in the quantity of labour that a certain quantity of corn can buy. But a rent reserved in any other commodity is liable not only to the variations in the quantity of labour that a particular quantity of corn can buy, but also to the variations in the quantity of corn that can be bought by a particular quantity of that commodity.

It should be noted, however, that although the real value of a corn rent varies much less from century to century than that of a money rent, it varies much more from year to year. The money price of labour, as I shall try to show later, does not fluctuate from year to year with the money price of corn, but seems to be everywhere adjusted not to the temporary or occasional price of that necessity of life, but to its average or ordinary price. The average or ordinary price of corn, again, is governed, as I shall also try to show later, by the value of silver—by the richness or poverty of the mines that supply the market with that metal, or by the quantity of labour that must be employed, and consequently of corn that must be consumed, in order to bring a particular quantity of silver from the mine to the market. But the value of silver, though it sometimes varies greatly from century to century, seldom varies much from year to year, and frequently stays the same, or very nearly the same, for half a century or a century at a stretch. The ordinary or average money price of corn, therefore, may over so long a period stay the same, or very nearly the same, and along with it the money price of labour, provided at least that the society remains in other respects in the same, or nearly the same, condition. Meanwhile, the temporary and occasional price of corn may frequently be double in one year of what it was the year before, fluctuating, for example, from twenty-five to fifty shillings the quarter. But when corn is at the latter price, not only the nominal but the real value of a corn rent will be double of what it is at the former, or will command double the quantity either of labour or of most other commodities; the money price of labour, and with it that of most other things, staying the same throughout all these fluctuations.

Labour, then, it plainly appears, is the only universal as well as the only accurate measure of value, the only standard by which we can compare the values of different commodities at all times and in all places. We cannot, it is granted, estimate the real value of different commodities from century to century by the quantities of silver given for them. We cannot estimate it from year to year by the quantities of corn. By the quantities of labour, we can estimate it with the greatest accuracy, both from century to century and from year to year. From century to century, corn is a better measure than silver, because from century to century equal quantities of corn will command the same quantity of labour more nearly than equal quantities of silver. From year to year, on the contrary, silver is a better measure than corn, because equal quantities of it will more nearly command the same quantity of labour.

But although, in setting up perpetual rents, or even in granting very long leases, it may be useful to distinguish between real and nominal price, it is of no use in buying and selling, the more common and ordinary transactions of human life.

At the same time and place, the real and the nominal price of all commodities are exactly in proportion to one another. The more or less money you get for any commodity in the London market, for example, the more or less labour it will at that time and place enable you to buy or command. At the same time and place, therefore, money is the exact measure of the real exchangeable value of all commodities. But it is so only at the same time and place.

Although at distant places there is no fixed proportion between the real and the money price of commodities, the merchant who carries goods from one to the other has nothing to consider but the money price—that is, the difference between the quantity of silver for which he buys them and that for which he is likely to sell them. Half an ounce of silver at Canton in China may command a greater quantity both of labour and of the necessities and comforts of life than an ounce at London. A commodity, therefore, that sells for half an ounce of silver at Canton may there be really dearer—of more real importance to the man who owns it there—than a commodity selling for an ounce at London is to the man who owns it at London. If a London merchant, however, can buy at Canton for half an ounce of silver a commodity he can afterwards sell at London for an ounce, he gains a hundred per cent by the bargain, just as much as if an ounce of silver were at London exactly of the same value as at Canton. It makes no difference to him that half an ounce of silver at Canton would have given him command of more labour, and of a greater quantity of the necessities and comforts of life, than an ounce can at London. An ounce at London will always give him command of double the quantity of all these things that half an ounce could have given there, and this is precisely what he wants.

Since it is the nominal or money price of goods, therefore, that finally decides the wisdom or folly of all purchases and sales, and so governs almost the whole business of everyday life in which price is concerned, it is no wonder that it should have been attended to so much more than the real price.

In a work like this, however, it may sometimes be useful to compare the different real values of a particular commodity at different times and places, or the different degrees of power over other people's labour that it may, on different occasions, have given to those who owned it. In this case we must compare, not so much the different quantities of silver for which it was commonly sold, as the different quantities of labour that those different quantities of silver could have bought. But the current prices of labour at distant times and places can scarcely ever be known with any degree of exactness. Those of corn, though they have been regularly recorded in few places, are in general better known and have been noted more often by historians and other writers. We must generally, therefore, content ourselves with them—not as being always in exactly the same proportion as the current prices of labour, but as being the nearest approximation that can commonly be had to that proportion. I shall later have occasion to make several comparisons of this kind.

As industry advanced, commercial nations found it convenient to coin several different metals into money: gold for larger payments, silver for purchases of moderate value, and copper, or some other coarse metal, for those of still smaller value. They have always, however, regarded one of those metals as more particularly the measure of value than either of the other two; and this preference seems generally to have been given to the metal they happened first to use as the instrument of trade. Having once begun to use it as their standard—which they must have done when they had no other money—they have generally continued to do so even when the necessity was no longer the same.

The Romans are said to have had nothing but copper money until within five years before the first Punic war (Pliny, book xxxiii, chapter 3), when they first began to coin silver. Copper, therefore, appears to have continued always the measure of value in that republic. At Rome all accounts seem to have been kept, and the value of all estates computed, either in asses or in sestertii. The as was always the denomination of a copper coin. The word sestertius means two asses and a half. So although the sestertius was originally a silver coin, its value was reckoned in copper. At Rome, a man who owed a great deal of money was said to have a great deal of other people's copper.

The northern nations that established themselves on the ruins of the Roman empire seem to have had silver money from the very beginning of their settlements, and not to have known either gold or copper coins for several ages afterwards. There were silver coins in England in the time of the Saxons; but little gold was coined until the time of Edward III, nor any copper until that of James I of Great Britain. In England, therefore—and for the same reason, I believe, in all the other modern nations of Europe—all accounts are kept, and the value of all goods and of all estates is generally computed, in silver; and when we mean to express the size of a person's fortune, we seldom mention the number of guineas, but the number of pounds sterling we suppose would be given for it.

Originally, in all countries, I believe, a legal tender of payment could be made only in the coin of the metal that was particularly regarded as the standard or measure of value. In England, gold was not regarded as legal tender for a long time after it was coined into money. The ratio between the values of gold and silver money was not fixed by any public law or proclamation, but was left to be settled by the market. If a debtor offered payment in gold, the creditor might either refuse such payment altogether or accept it at whatever valuation of the gold he and his debtor could agree on. Copper is not at present legal tender, except in making change for the smaller silver coins.
In this state of things, the distinction between the metal that was the standard and the metal that was not was something more than a merely nominal distinction.

In time, as people gradually became more familiar with the use of the different metals in coin, and so better acquainted with the ratio between their respective values, it has in most countries, I believe, been found convenient to fix this ratio and to declare by a public law that a guinea, for example, of such a weight and fineness should exchange for twenty-one shillings, or be legal tender for a debt of that amount. In this state of things, and so long as any one regulated ratio of this kind continues, the distinction between the metal that is the standard and the metal that is not becomes little more than a nominal distinction.

As a result of any change, however, in this regulated ratio, this distinction becomes—or at least seems to become—something more than nominal again. If the regulated value of a guinea, for example, were either reduced to twenty or raised to twenty-two shillings, then, since all accounts are kept and almost all debt obligations expressed in silver money, the greater part of payments could in either case be made with the same quantity of silver money as before, but would require very different quantities of gold money—more in the one case, less in the other. Silver would appear more invariable in its value than gold. Silver would appear to measure the value of gold, and gold would not appear to measure the value of silver. The value of gold would seem to depend on the quantity of silver it would exchange for, and the value of silver would not seem to depend on the quantity of gold it would exchange for. This difference, however, would be entirely due to the custom of keeping accounts, and of expressing the amount of all sums large and small, in silver rather than in gold money. One of Mr Drummond's notes for twenty-five or fifty guineas would, after an alteration of this kind, still be payable with twenty-five or fifty guineas, just as before. After such an alteration it would be payable with the same quantity of gold as before, but with very different quantities of silver. In the payment of such a note, gold would appear more invariable in its value than silver. Gold would appear to measure the value of silver, and silver would not appear to measure the value of gold. If the custom of keeping accounts, and of expressing promissory notes and other money obligations, in this manner were ever to become general, gold, and not silver, would be regarded as the metal that was particularly the standard or measure of value.

In reality, so long as any one regulated ratio between the respective values of the different metals in coin continues, the value of the most precious metal governs the value of the whole coinage. Twelve copper pence contain half a pound avoirdupois of copper, of not the best quality, which before it is coined is seldom worth seven-pence in silver. But because, by the regulation, twelve such pence are required to exchange for a shilling, they are in the market treated as worth a shilling, and a shilling can at any time be had for them. Even before the recent reform of the gold coin of Great Britain, the gold—at least the part of it that circulated in London and its neighbourhood—was in general less degraded below its standard weight than the greater part of the silver. Twenty-one worn and defaced shillings, however, were treated as equivalent to a guinea, which perhaps was itself worn and defaced too, but seldom so much. The recent regulations have brought the gold coin as near to its standard weight, perhaps, as it is possible to bring the current coin of any nation; and the order to receive no gold at the public offices except by weight is likely to keep it so, as long as that order is enforced. The silver coin still remains in the same worn and degraded state as before the reform of the gold coin. In the market, however, twenty-one shillings of this degraded silver coin are still treated as worth a guinea of this excellent gold coin.
The reform of the gold coin has evidently raised the value of the silver coin that can be exchanged for it.

In the English mint, a pound weight of gold is coined into forty-four and a half guineas, which at twenty-one shillings to the guinea is equal to forty-six pounds fourteen shillings and sixpence. An ounce of such gold coin, therefore, is worth £3 17s 10½d in silver. In England no duty or seignorage is paid on the coinage, and a man who carries a pound weight or an ounce weight of standard gold bullion to the mint gets back a pound weight or an ounce weight of gold in coin, without any deduction. Three pounds seventeen shillings and tenpence halfpenny an ounce, therefore, is said to be the mint price of gold in England—that is, the quantity of gold coin the mint gives in return for standard gold bullion.

Before the reform of the gold coin, the market price of standard gold bullion had for many years been above £3 18s, sometimes £3 19s, and very frequently £4 an ounce; and that sum, in the worn and degraded gold coin, probably seldom contained more than an ounce of standard gold. Since the reform of the gold coin, the market price of standard gold bullion seldom exceeds £3 17s 7d an ounce. Before the reform of the gold coin, the market price was always more or less above the mint price. Since that reform, the market price has been constantly below the mint price. But that market price is the same whether it is paid in gold or in silver coin.
