The recent reform of the gold coin, therefore, has raised not only the value of the gold coin but likewise that of the silver coin in proportion to gold bullion, and probably too in proportion to all other commodities; though, since the price of most other commodities is influenced by so many other causes, the rise in the value of either gold or silver coin in proportion to them may not be so distinct and noticeable.

In the English mint, a pound weight of standard silver bullion is coined into sixty-two shillings, containing, in the same way, a pound weight of standard silver. Five shillings and twopence an ounce, therefore, is said to be the mint price of silver in England—that is, the quantity of silver coin the mint gives in return for standard silver bullion. Before the reform of the gold coin, the market price of standard silver bullion was, on different occasions, five shillings and fourpence, five shillings and fivepence, five shillings and sixpence, five shillings and sevenpence, and very often five shillings and eightpence an ounce. Five shillings and sevenpence, however, seems to have been the most common price. Since the reform of the gold coin, the market price of standard silver bullion has fallen occasionally to five shillings and threepence, five shillings and fourpence, and five shillings and fivepence an ounce, the last of which it has scarcely ever exceeded. Although the market price of silver bullion has fallen considerably since the reform of the gold coin, it has not fallen as low as the mint price.

In the ratio between the different metals in the English coin, just as copper is rated far above its real value, so silver is rated somewhat below it. In the market of Europe—in the French coin and in the Dutch coin—an ounce of fine gold exchanges for about fourteen ounces of fine silver. In the English coin it exchanges for about fifteen ounces, that is, for more silver than it is worth according to the common reckoning of Europe. But just as the price of copper in bars is not, even in England, raised by the high price of copper in English coin, so the price of silver in bullion is not lowered by the low rate of silver in English coin. Silver in bullion still keeps its proper proportion to gold, for the same reason that copper in bars keeps its proper proportion to silver.

On the reform of the silver coin in the reign of William III, the price of silver bullion still continued to be somewhat above the mint price. Mr Locke attributed this high price to the permission to export silver bullion and the prohibition against exporting silver coin. This permission to export, he said, made the demand for silver bullion greater than the demand for silver coin. But the number of people who want silver coin for the common purposes of buying and selling at home is surely much greater than the number who want silver bullion either for export or for any other use. There exists at present a similar permission to export gold bullion, and a similar prohibition against exporting gold coin; and yet the price of gold bullion has fallen below the mint price. But in the English coin, silver was then, just as now, under-rated in proportion to gold; and the gold coin (which at that time too was not supposed to need any reform) governed then, as well as now, the real value of the whole coinage. Since the reform of the silver coin did not then reduce the price of silver bullion to the mint price, it is not very likely that a similar reform would do so now.

If the silver coin were brought back as near to its standard weight as the gold, a guinea, by the present ratio, would probably exchange for more silver in coin than it would buy in bullion. Since the silver coin would then contain its full standard weight, there would in that case be a profit in melting it down, in order first to sell the bullion for gold coin, and afterwards to exchange this gold coin for silver coin, to be melted down in the same way. Some alteration in the present ratio seems to be the only way of preventing this drawback.

The drawback, perhaps, would be less if silver were rated in the coin as much above its proper proportion to gold as it is at present rated below it, provided it were at the same time enacted that silver should not be legal tender for more than the change of a guinea—just as copper is not legal tender for more than the change of a shilling. No creditor could in that case be cheated by the high valuation of silver in coin, just as no creditor can at present be cheated by the high valuation of copper. The bankers alone would suffer by this regulation. When there is a run on them, they sometimes try to gain time by paying in sixpences, and this regulation would shut them out from this discreditable method of putting off immediate payment. They would consequently be obliged to keep at all times a greater quantity of cash in their coffers than at present; and though this might no doubt be a considerable inconvenience to them, it would at the same time be a considerable security to their creditors.

Three pounds seventeen shillings and tenpence halfpenny (the mint price of gold) certainly does not contain, even in our present excellent gold coin, more than an ounce of standard gold, and it might be thought, therefore, that it should not buy more standard bullion. But gold in coin is more convenient than gold in bullion; and although in England the coinage is free, yet the gold carried in bullion to the mint can seldom be returned in coin to the owner until after a delay of several weeks. In the present rush at the mint, it could not be returned until after a delay of several months. This delay is equivalent to a small duty, and makes gold in coin somewhat more valuable than an equal quantity of gold in bullion. If, in the English coin, silver were rated according to its proper proportion to gold, the price of silver bullion would probably fall below the mint price, even without any reform of the silver coin; the value even of the present worn and defaced silver coin being governed by the value of the excellent gold coin for which it can be exchanged.

A small seignorage or duty on the coinage of both gold and silver would probably increase still further the superiority of those metals in coin over an equal quantity of either of them in bullion. The coinage would in that case increase the value of the metal coined in proportion to the size of this small duty, for the same reason that the workmanship increases the value of plate in proportion to the cost of that workmanship. The superiority of coin over bullion would prevent the melting down of the coin, and would discourage its export. If, on any public emergency, it should become necessary to export the coin, the greater part of it would soon return again of its own accord. Abroad, it could sell only for its weight in bullion. At home, it would buy more than that weight. There would be a profit, therefore, in bringing it home again. In France, a seignorage of about eight per cent is imposed on the coinage, and the French coin, when exported, is said to return home again of its own accord.

The occasional fluctuations in the market price of gold and silver bullion arise from the same causes as the like fluctuations in the price of all other commodities. The frequent loss of those metals through various accidents by sea and by land, the continual waste of them in gilding and plating, in lace and embroidery, in the wear and tear of coin and of plate, all require, in every country that has no mines of its own, a continual importation in order to repair this loss and waste. The importing merchants, like all other merchants, we may believe, try as best they can to match their occasional imports to what they judge is likely to be the immediate demand. With all their care, however, they sometimes overdo it and sometimes underdo it. When they import more bullion than is wanted, rather than run the risk and trouble of exporting it again they are sometimes willing to sell part of it for something less than the ordinary or average price. When, on the other hand, they import less than is wanted, they get something more than this price. But when, despite all these occasional fluctuations, the market price of either gold or silver bullion continues for several years together steadily and constantly either more or less above, or more or less below, the mint price, we may be sure that this steady and constant superiority or inferiority of price is the effect of something in the state of the coin which at that time makes a certain quantity of coin either of more value or of less value than the precise quantity of bullion it ought to contain. The constancy and steadiness of the effect presupposes a corresponding constancy and steadiness in the cause.

The money of any particular country is, at any particular time and place, a more or less accurate measure of value, depending on how exactly the current coin conforms to its standard, or contains the precise quantity of pure gold or pure silver it ought to contain. If in England, for example, forty-four and a half guineas contained exactly a pound weight of standard gold, or eleven ounces of fine gold and one ounce of alloy, the gold coin of England would be as accurate a measure of the actual value of goods at any particular time and place as the nature of the thing would allow. But if, by rubbing and wearing, forty-four and a half guineas generally contain less than a pound weight of standard gold—the reduction, moreover, being greater in some pieces than in others—the measure of value comes to be liable to the same sort of uncertainty to which all other weights and measures are commonly exposed. Since it rarely happens that these conform exactly to their standard, the merchant adjusts the price of his goods as well as he can, not to what those weights and measures ought to be, but to what, on an average, he finds by experience they actually are. As a result of a similar disorder in the coin, the price of goods comes in the same way to be adjusted not to the quantity of pure gold or silver the coin ought to contain, but to the quantity that, on an average, it is found by experience actually to contain.

By the money price of goods, it should be noted, I always understand the quantity of pure gold or silver for which they are sold, without any regard to the denomination of the coin. Six shillings and eightpence, for example, in the time of Edward I, I regard as the same money price as a pound sterling in the present day, because it contained, as nearly as we can judge, the same quantity of pure silver.

title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: On the Component Parts of the Price of Commodities.

In that early and primitive state of society, before any accumulation of capital and before land became private property, the ratio between the amounts of labour needed to obtain different things seems to be the only thing that can set a rule for exchanging them with one another. If, for example, among a nation of hunters it usually takes twice as much labour to kill a beaver as it does to kill a deer, then one beaver should naturally exchange for, or be worth, two deer. It makes sense that whatever is normally the product of two days' or two hours' labour should be worth twice as much as whatever is normally the product of one day's or one hour's labour.

If one kind of labour is harder than the other, some allowance will naturally be made for that extra hardship, and the product of one hour's labour in one trade may often exchange for the product of two hours' labour in another.

Or if one kind of labour calls for an unusual degree of skill and ingenuity, the respect people have for such talents will naturally give their product a value higher than what the time spent would alone deserve. Such talents can rarely be acquired except through long practice, and the extra value of what they produce may often be no more than fair compensation for the time and effort that must go into acquiring them. In an advanced society, allowances of this kind, for greater hardship and greater skill, are routinely built into the wages of labour, and something similar must probably have existed even in society's earliest and most primitive period.

In this state of things, the entire product of labour belongs to the labourer, and the amount of labour normally needed to acquire or produce any commodity is the only thing that can determine how much labour it ought normally to buy, command, or exchange for.

As soon as capital has built up in the hands of particular individuals, some of them will naturally use it to set industrious people to work, supplying them with materials and a living so as to make a profit from selling their output, or from what their labour adds to the value of the materials. When the finished product is exchanged for money, for labour, or for other goods, something beyond what is needed to cover the cost of the materials and the workers' wages must be given as profit to the undertaker of the work, who risks his capital on the venture. The value the workers add to the materials therefore divides, in this case, into two parts: one pays their wages, and the other pays the profits of their employer on the whole stock of materials and wages that he advanced. He would have no reason to employ them unless he expected the sale of their work to bring in something more than enough to restore his capital to him, and no reason to employ a large stock rather than a small one unless his profits were to bear some proportion to the size of that stock.

It might perhaps be thought that the profits of capital are merely another name for the wages of a particular kind of labour, namely the labour of supervision and management. They are, however, entirely different; they are governed by quite different principles, and they bear no relation to the amount, the hardship, or the ingenuity of this supposed labour of supervision and management. They are governed entirely by the value of the capital employed, and they are larger or smaller in proportion to the size of that capital. Suppose, for example, that in some particular place, where the usual annual profit on manufacturing capital is ten per cent, there are two different manufactures, each employing twenty workers at fifteen pounds a year each, or at a cost of three hundred a year in each factory. Suppose, too, that the coarse materials worked up annually in one factory cost only seven hundred pounds, while the finer materials in the other cost seven thousand. The capital employed annually in the first will then amount to only one thousand pounds, whereas that employed in the other will amount to seven thousand three hundred pounds. At a rate of ten per cent, therefore, the undertaker of the first will expect a yearly profit of only about one hundred pounds, while the undertaker of the other will expect about seven hundred and thirty pounds. Yet although their profits differ so greatly, their labour of supervision and management may be either exactly or very nearly the same. In many large operations almost all labour of this kind is handed over to some principal clerk, whose wages properly represent the value of this labour of supervision and management. Although in fixing those wages some account is usually taken not only of his work and skill but also of the trust placed in him, they never bear any regular proportion to the capital whose management he oversees; and the owner of that capital, though he is thus relieved of nearly all the labour, still expects his profit to bear a regular proportion to his capital. In the price of commodities, therefore, the profits of capital make up a component part entirely distinct from the wages of labour and governed by quite different principles.

In this state of things, the whole product of labour does not always belong to the labourer. In most cases he has to share it with the owner of the capital that employs him. Nor is the amount of labour normally needed to acquire or produce any commodity the only thing that can determine how much labour it ought normally to buy, command, or exchange for. Clearly, an additional amount must be owed for the profits of the capital that advanced the wages and supplied the materials for that labour.

As soon as all the land of a country has become private property, the landlords, like everyone else, are fond of reaping where they never sowed, and they demand a rent even for the land's natural produce. The timber of the forest, the grass of the field, and all the natural fruits of the earth, which, when land was held in common, cost the labourer only the trouble of gathering them, come to have an extra price set on them, even for him. He must then pay for permission to gather them, and he must hand over to the landlord a share of whatever his labour collects or produces. This share, or what amounts to the same thing, the price of this share, makes up the rent of land, and in the price of most commodities it forms a third component part.

It must be noted that the real value of all the different component parts of price is measured by the amount of labour that each of them can buy or command. Labour measures the value not only of the part of price that resolves into labour, but also of the part that resolves into rent and the part that resolves into profit.

In every society, the price of every commodity ultimately resolves into some one, or some other, or all of those three parts; and in every advanced society all three enter, to a greater or lesser degree, as component parts into the price of the great majority of commodities.

In the price of corn, for example, one part pays the landlord's rent, another pays the wages or upkeep of the labourers and the working cattle used in producing it, and the third pays the farmer's profit. These three parts seem, either directly or ultimately, to make up the whole price of corn. It might perhaps be thought that a fourth part is needed to replace the farmer's stock, or to make up for the wear and tear on his working cattle and other farming tools. But consider that the price of any farming tool, such as a working horse, is itself made up of the same three parts: the rent of the land on which he is raised, the labour of tending and rearing him, and the profit of the farmer, who advances both the rent of that land and the wages of that labour. So although the price of the corn may pay both the price and the upkeep of the horse, the whole price still resolves, either directly or ultimately, into the same three parts of rent, labour, and profit.

In the price of flour or meal we must add to the price of the corn the miller's profits and the wages of his servants; in the price of bread, the baker's profits and the wages of his servants; and in the price of both, the labour of carrying the corn from the farmer's house to the miller's, and from the miller's to the baker's, together with the profits of those who advance the wages for that labour.

The price of flax resolves into the same three parts as the price of corn. In the price of linen we must add to that price the wages of the flax-dresser, the spinner, the weaver, the bleacher, and so on, together with the profits of their various employers.

As any particular commodity becomes more manufactured, the part of the price that resolves into wages and profit grows larger in proportion to the part that resolves into rent. As the manufacturing process advances, not only does the number of profits increase, but each later profit is greater than the one before it, because the capital from which it comes must always be larger. The capital that employs the weavers, for instance, must be larger than the one that employs the spinners, because it not only replaces that earlier capital along with its profits but also pays the wages of the weavers; and profits must always bear some proportion to the capital.

In the most advanced societies, however, there are always a few commodities whose price resolves into only two parts, the wages of labour and the profits of capital, and a still smaller number whose price consists entirely of the wages of labour. In the price of sea-fish, for example, one part pays the labour of the fisherman, and the other the profits of the capital employed in the fishery. Rent very rarely makes up any part of it, though it sometimes does, as I shall show later. The case is different, at least throughout most of Europe, with river fisheries. A salmon fishery pays a rent; and that rent, though it cannot strictly be called the rent of land, forms part of the price of a salmon, along with wages and profit. In some parts of Scotland a few poor people make a living by gathering, along the seashore, those little speckled stones commonly known as Scotch pebbles. The price the stone-cutter pays them is entirely the wages of their labour; neither rent nor profit makes up any part of it.

But the whole price of any commodity must still ultimately resolve into some one, or some other, or all of those three parts; for whatever part of it is left after paying the rent of the land and the price of all the labour spent in raising, manufacturing, and bringing it to market must necessarily be profit for somebody.

Just as the price or exchangeable value of every particular commodity, taken on its own, resolves into some one, or some other, or all of those three parts, so the value of all the commodities that together make up a country's whole annual product of labour, taken as a whole, must resolve into the same three parts and be divided among the country's various inhabitants, either as the wages of their labour, the profits of their capital, or the rent of their land. The whole of what is annually collected or produced by the labour of any society, or, what amounts to the same thing, the whole price of it, is in this way originally distributed among some of its different members. Wages, profit, and rent are the three original sources of all revenue, as well as of all exchangeable value. Every other kind of revenue is ultimately drawn from one or another of these.

Whoever draws his revenue from a fund that is his own must draw it either from his labour, from his capital, or from his land. The revenue drawn from labour is called wages; the revenue drawn from capital by the person who manages or employs it is called profit; the revenue drawn from it by the person who does not employ it himself but lends it to another is called the interest or use of money. Interest is the compensation the borrower pays the lender for the profit that the borrower has an opportunity of making by using the money. Part of that profit naturally belongs to the borrower, who runs the risk and takes the trouble of employing it, and part to the lender, who gives him the chance to make this profit. The interest of money is always a derivative revenue, which, if it is not paid out of the profit made by using the money, must be paid out of some other source of revenue, unless perhaps the borrower is a spendthrift who takes on a second debt in order to pay the interest on the first. The revenue that comes entirely from land is called rent, and it belongs to the landlord. The farmer's revenue comes partly from his labour and partly from his capital. To him, land is only the instrument that enables him to earn the wages of this labour and to make the profits of this capital. All taxes, and all the revenue founded on them, all salaries, pensions, and annuities of every kind, are ultimately drawn from one or another of those three original sources of revenue, and are paid either directly or indirectly out of the wages of labour, the profits of capital, or the rent of land.

When those three different kinds of revenue belong to different people, they are easily told apart; but when they belong to the same person, they are sometimes confused with one another, at least in everyday speech.

A gentleman who farms part of his own estate should, after paying the cost of cultivation, gain both the landlord's rent and the farmer's profit. He is inclined, however, to call his whole gain profit, and so confuses rent with profit, at least in everyday speech. Most of our North American and West Indian planters are in this situation. The greater part of them farm their own estates, and so we seldom hear of the rent of a plantation, but frequently of its profit.

Common farmers seldom employ any overseer to direct the general operations of the farm. They also generally do a good deal of the work with their own hands, as ploughmen, harrowers, and so on. What is left of the crop after paying the rent should therefore not only replace the capital they employed in cultivation, along with its ordinary profits, but also pay them the wages owed to them both as labourers and as overseers. Yet whatever is left after paying the rent and maintaining the capital is called profit. But wages clearly make up part of it. By saving these wages, the farmer must necessarily gain them. In this case, then, wages are confused with profit.

An independent manufacturer who has capital enough both to buy materials and to support himself until he can bring his work to market should gain both the wages of a journeyman working under a master and the profit that the master makes by selling that journeyman's work. His whole gains, however, are usually called profit, and here too wages are confused with profit.

A gardener who cultivates his own garden with his own hands combines in himself the three different characters of landlord, farmer, and labourer. His produce should therefore pay him the rent owed to the first, the profit owed to the second, and the wages owed to the third. Yet the whole is usually regarded as the earnings of his labour. In this case, both rent and profit are confused with wages.

Since in a civilized country there are only a few commodities whose exchangeable value comes from labour alone, with rent and profit contributing largely to the value of most of them, the annual product of a country's labour will always be enough to buy or command a much greater quantity of labour than was used in raising, preparing, and bringing that product to market. If the society were to employ each year all the labour it can annually buy, then, since the quantity of labour would grow greatly every year, the product of each succeeding year would be of vastly greater value than that of the year before. But there is no country in which the whole annual product is used to maintain the industrious. The idle everywhere consume a large part of it; and depending on the different proportions in which it is annually divided between these two different sorts of people, its ordinary or average value must either increase from year to year, or decrease, or stay the same.

title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: The Natural and Market Price of Commodities

In every society or local area there is an ordinary, average rate of wages and of profit for each different kind of work and each different use of capital. As I'll explain later, this rate is shaped by two things. One is the general condition of the society—whether it is rich or poor, and whether it is growing, holding steady, or declining. The other is the particular nature of each kind of employment.

There is likewise an ordinary, average rate of rent in every society or area. As I'll also explain later, this rate is shaped partly by the general condition of the place where the land sits, and partly by how fertile the land is, whether naturally or through improvement.
We can call these ordinary or average rates the natural rates of wages, profit, and rent for the particular time and place where they normally hold.

Suppose the price of some product is exactly enough to cover the rent of the land, the wages of the labor, and the profit on the capital used to grow it, prepare it, and bring it to market, each at its natural rate. That product is then selling at what we can call its natural price.

At that price the product is selling for exactly what it is worth—for what it actually costs the person who brings it to market. In everyday speech, the so-called prime cost of a product doesn't include the seller's profit. Yet if he sells at a price that doesn't give him the ordinary rate of profit for his area, he is clearly losing money on the deal, because he could have earned that profit by putting his capital to some other use. On top of that, his profit is his income, the fund he lives on. While he is preparing the goods and bringing them to market, he advances his workers their wages, that is, their means of living. In the same way he advances himself his own means of living, an amount that normally matches the profit he can reasonably expect from selling his goods. So unless the goods yield him that profit, they don't pay him back what they can fairly be said to have actually cost him.

The price that leaves him this profit isn't always the lowest at which a dealer will sometimes sell. But it is the lowest at which he is likely to keep selling for any length of time—at least where there is complete freedom to act, and where he can switch trades as often as he likes.
The price a product actually and normally sells for is called its market price. It can be above its natural price, below it, or exactly equal to it.

The market price of any particular product is set by the relationship between two things: the quantity actually brought to market, and the demand from people willing to pay the natural price—that is, the full value of the rent, labor, and profit that must be paid to bring it there. We can call these people the effectual demanders, and their demand the effectual demand, because it can actually bring about getting the product to market. This is different from absolute demand. In some sense a very poor man can be said to have a demand for a coach and six horses; he might like to own one. But his is not an effectual demand, since the product can never be brought to market just to satisfy it.

When the quantity brought to market falls short of the effectual demand, not everyone willing to pay the full rent, wages, and profit can get as much as they want. Rather than go without entirely, some of them will be willing to pay more. Competition immediately breaks out among them, and the market price rises above the natural price by more or less, depending on how large the shortage is and on how much the wealth and reckless luxury of the bidders sharpen their eagerness. Among bidders of equal wealth and luxury, the same shortage usually stirs up keener or milder competition depending on how badly each one wants the product. This is why the necessities of life reach outrageous prices during the blockade of a town or in a famine.

When the quantity brought to market is greater than the effectual demand, it can't all be sold to people willing to pay the full rent, wages, and profit needed to bring it there. Some of it must be sold to people willing to pay less, and the low price they pay drags down the price of the whole supply. The market price sinks below the natural price by more or less, depending on how much the surplus increases the sellers' competition, and on how urgent it is for them to unload the product right away. The same surplus causes far fiercer competition with perishable goods than with durable ones—with imported oranges, for instance, than with scrap iron.

When the quantity brought to market is just enough to meet the effectual demand and no more, the market price naturally settles at, or as close as can be judged to, the natural price. The whole stock on hand can be sold at this price, and can't be sold for more. Competition among the various dealers forces them all to accept this price, but doesn't force them to accept less.

The quantity of every product brought to market naturally adjusts itself to the effectual demand. Everyone who uses their land, labor, or capital to bring a product to market has an interest in keeping the quantity from ever exceeding the effectual demand; and everyone else has an interest in its never falling short of that demand.

Whenever the supply exceeds the effectual demand, some part of the price must be paid below its natural rate. If it's rent, landlords' self-interest will quickly push them to pull some of their land out of that use. If it's wages or profit, the self-interest of the workers in the one case, and of their employers in the other, will push them to pull some of their labor or capital out of that line of work. The quantity brought to market soon shrinks to no more than enough to meet the effectual demand. Every component of the price climbs back to its natural rate, and the whole price returns to its natural price.

If instead the supply falls short of the effectual demand, some part of the price must rise above its natural rate. If it's rent, other landlords will naturally be prompted to prepare more land for growing that product. If it's wages or profit, other workers and dealers will soon be prompted to put more labor and capital into preparing it and bringing it to market. The quantity brought there soon grows enough to meet the effectual demand. Every component of the price soon sinks back to its natural rate, and the whole price returns to its natural price.

So the natural price is, in effect, the central price toward which the prices of all products are continually pulled. Various accidents may sometimes hold them well above it, and sometimes force them somewhat below it. But whatever obstacles keep them from settling at this point of rest and stability, they are always tending toward it.

The total amount of industry employed each year to bring any product to market naturally adjusts itself this way to the effectual demand. It naturally aims always to bring exactly the quantity that will meet that demand and no more.

But in some lines of work the same amount of industry produces very different quantities in different years, while in others it produces always the same, or very nearly the same. The same number of farm workers will, in different years, produce very different quantities of grain, wine, oil, hops, and so on. But the same number of spinners or weavers will every year produce the same, or very nearly the same, quantity of linen and woolen cloth. Only the average output of the first kind of industry can match the effectual demand at all; and since its actual output is often much larger and often much smaller than its average, the quantity brought to market sometimes far exceeds and sometimes falls far short of the effectual demand. So even if that demand always stayed the same, the market price would still swing widely, sometimes dropping well below and sometimes rising well above the natural price. In the second kind of industry, where equal amounts of labor always produce the same or nearly the same output, supply can be matched to the effectual demand more precisely. As long as that demand holds steady, the market price of these goods is likely to hold steady too, staying either exactly at the natural price or as close to it as can be judged. Everyone's own experience tells them that the price of linen and woolen cloth doesn't vary as often or as much as the price of grain. The price of the first kind of goods varies only with changes in demand; the price of the second varies not only with changes in demand but with the much greater and more frequent changes in the quantity brought to market to meet that demand.

The occasional, temporary swings in a product's market price fall mainly on the parts of its price that come down to wages and profit. The part that comes down to rent is less affected by them. A rent fixed in money isn't affected at all, in either its rate or its value. A rent paid as a fixed share, or a fixed quantity, of the raw produce certainly has its yearly value affected by every occasional and temporary swing in the market price of that produce; but its yearly rate is rarely affected. When setting the terms of the lease, landlord and farmer do their best to fix that rate not by the temporary, occasional price of the produce but by its average, ordinary price.

These swings affect both the value and the rate of wages or profit, depending on whether the market happens to be overstocked or understocked—with goods or with labor, with work already done or with work still to be done. A period of public mourning raises the price of black cloth, which the market is almost always short of on such occasions, and increases the profits of merchants holding any sizable stock of it. It has no effect on the weavers' wages: here the market is short of goods, not of labor—of work already done, not of work still to be done. The same mourning raises the wages of journeyman tailors. Here the market is short of labor: there's an effectual demand for more labor, more work to be done, than can be supplied. And it lowers the price of colored silks and cloths, cutting the profits of merchants holding any large stock of them. It also lowers the wages of the workers who make such goods, since all demand for them stops for six months, maybe a full year. Here the market is overstocked both with goods and with labor.

But although the market price of every particular product is continually pulled, so to speak, toward the natural price, sometimes particular accidents, sometimes natural causes, and sometimes particular government regulations can, for many goods, hold the market price well above the natural price for a long stretch of time.

When a rise in effectual demand pushes the market price of some product well above its natural price, the people supplying that market are usually careful to hide the change. If it were widely known, their large profit would tempt so many new rivals to put their capital into the same business that the effectual demand would soon be fully met, and the market price would soon fall back to the natural price, and perhaps for a while even below it. If the market is far from where the suppliers live, they can sometimes keep the secret for several years running and enjoy their extraordinary profits that long without new rivals. Still, it must be admitted that secrets of this kind can rarely be kept for long, and the extraordinary profit lasts barely any longer than the secret does.

Secrets in manufacturing can be kept longer than secrets in trade. A dyer who has found a way to make a particular color using materials that cost only half the usual price may, with good management, enjoy the benefit of his discovery for the rest of his life and even leave it to his descendants. His extraordinary earnings come from the high price paid for his private skill. Properly speaking they are the high wages of that labor. But because those earnings recur on every part of his capital, and their total therefore bears a regular proportion to it, they are usually counted as extraordinary profits on capital.
Such increases in the market price are clearly the result of particular accidents, though their effect can sometimes last for many years on end.

Some natural products require such a rare combination of soil and location that all the land in a large country suited to producing them may not be enough to meet the effectual demand. The whole quantity brought to market can therefore be sold to people willing to pay more than enough to cover the rent of the land that produced it, plus the wages of the labor and the profits of the capital used to prepare it and bring it to market, each at its natural rate. Such goods can keep selling at this high price for whole centuries; and in this case the part of the price that comes down to land rent is the part generally paid above its natural rate. The rent of land that yields such rare and prized products—like the rent of some French vineyards with a uniquely fortunate soil and location—bears no regular proportion to the rent of other equally fertile and equally well-cultivated land nearby. The wages of labor and the profits of capital used to bring such goods to market, by contrast, are seldom out of their natural proportion to those in other employments of labor and capital nearby.
Such increases in the market price are clearly the result of natural causes, which may keep the effectual demand from ever being fully met, and which may therefore go on operating forever.

A monopoly granted to an individual or a trading company has the same effect as a secret in trade or manufacturing. By keeping the market constantly understocked, never fully meeting the effectual demand, the monopolists sell their goods well above the natural price and push their returns—whether wages or profit—far above their natural rate.

The monopoly price is always the highest that can be got. The natural price, the price under free competition, is by contrast the lowest that can be taken—not on every single occasion, but over any considerable stretch of time. The monopoly price is always the highest that can be squeezed out of buyers, or that they are thought willing to give; the natural price is the lowest that sellers can normally afford to take while staying in business.

The exclusive privileges of corporations, the statutes of apprenticeship, and all the laws that limit competition in particular trades to fewer people than would otherwise enter them, work in the same direction, though less strongly. They are a kind of enlarged monopoly, and they can often, for ages on end and across whole classes of employment, hold the market price of particular goods above the natural price and keep both the wages of labor and the profits of capital involved somewhat above their natural rate.
Such increases in the market price can last as long as the regulations that give rise to them.

The market price of any particular product, though it can stay above its natural price for a long time, can rarely stay below it for long. Whatever part of the price was paid below the natural rate, the people whose interest it touched would feel the loss at once and would immediately pull so much land, or labor, or capital out of that use that the quantity brought to market would soon be no more than enough to meet the effectual demand. Its market price would therefore soon rise to the natural price—at least where there is complete freedom.

The very statutes of apprenticeship and other corporation laws that let a worker raise his wages well above their natural rate while a trade is prosperous sometimes force him, when it declines, to let his wages drop well below it. In the one case they shut many people out of his trade; in the other they shut him out of many trades. Yet these regulations don't drive a worker's wages below the natural rate nearly as durably as they raise them above it. Their effect in raising wages can last for many centuries, but in lowering them it can last no longer than the lives of some of the workers trained in the trade during its prosperity. Once they are gone, the number of people later trained for the trade naturally adjusts itself to the effectual demand. It would take a policy as harsh as that of Hindustan or ancient Egypt—where every man was bound by religious principle to follow his father's occupation and was supposed to commit the most horrible sacrilege if he changed it—to push the wages of labor or the profits of capital, in any particular trade and for several generations running, below their natural rate.
This is all I think needs noting at present about the ways, whether occasional or permanent, in which the market price of goods departs from the natural price.

The natural price itself varies with the natural rate of each of its parts—wages, profit, and rent—and in every society these rates vary with its circumstances: with its wealth or poverty, and with whether it is growing, holding steady, or declining. In the next four chapters I'll try to explain, as fully and clearly as I can, the causes of these different variations.

First, I'll try to explain the circumstances that naturally determine the rate of wages, and how those circumstances are affected by the wealth or poverty of a society and by its growing, stationary, or declining state.
Second, I'll try to show the circumstances that naturally determine the rate of profit, and how those circumstances too are affected by the same kinds of changes in the state of society.

Although money wages and profit differ greatly across the various employments of labor and capital, a certain proportion does seem to hold generally between money wages across all the different employments of labor and money profits across all the different employments of capital. This proportion, as will appear later, depends partly on the nature of the different employments and partly on the different laws and policies of the society where they are carried on. But although it depends in many ways on laws and policy, this proportion seems little affected by whether the society is rich or poor, or growing, stationary, or declining; it stays the same, or very nearly the same, across all these different states. In the third place, I'll try to explain all the different circumstances that govern this proportion.
Fourth and last, I'll try to show the circumstances that govern the rent of land, and that either raise or lower the real price of all the different things the land produces.

title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: The Wages of Labour

What labour produces is its natural payment, or wages. In the original condition that came before anyone owned land or accumulated capital, the whole product of a person's labour belonged to that person. There was no landlord and no employer to take a share.

If that condition had continued, wages would have risen alongside every gain in productivity that the division of labour creates. Everything would gradually have grown cheaper, since each good would take less labour to make. And because goods made with equal amounts of labour would naturally trade for one another in such a world, you would also have been able to buy any given good with the product of less labour than before.

Yet even though everything would really have become cheaper, some things might have looked dearer than before, because they would trade for a larger quantity of other goods. Take an example. Suppose that in most jobs productivity rose tenfold, so that a day's work now produced ten times what it once did, but in one particular trade it rose only twofold, so that a day's work there produced merely twice what it once did. When you trade a day's output from the high-productivity jobs for a day's output from this one trade, ten times the original quantity of work in them buys only twice the original quantity in it. So a fixed amount of that one good — a pound of it, say — would seem five times dearer than before. In reality, though, it would be twice as cheap. Even though it now took five times as much of other goods to buy it, it would take only half as much labour either to buy it or to make it. Acquiring it would therefore be twice as easy as before.

But this original condition, in which the worker kept everything his labour produced, could not survive once people began to own land and accumulate capital. It was over, in other words, long before the great gains in productivity ever appeared. So there is no point tracing further what it might have meant for wages.
As soon as land becomes private property, the landlord demands a share of nearly everything the worker can grow or gather on it. His rent is the first cut taken from what farm labour produces.

The person who works the soil rarely has enough to live on until the harvest comes in. His upkeep is usually advanced to him out of the capital of an employer — the farmer who hires him — and that farmer would have no reason to hire him unless he too were to share in what the labour produced, or unless his capital came back to him with a profit. This profit is the second cut taken from what farm labour produces.

Almost all other labour is subject to the same deduction for profit. Across every craft and manufacture, most workers need an employer to advance them the raw materials, plus their wages and upkeep, until the job is done. He shares in what their labour produces — in the value it adds to the materials it is worked into — and that share is his profit.

Sometimes, of course, a single independent worker has enough capital both to buy his own materials and to support himself until the work is finished. He is at once employer and worker, and he keeps everything his labour produces, the whole value it adds to the materials. This income rolls together what are normally two separate revenues belonging to two separate people: the profits of capital and the wages of labour.

Such cases, however, are not common. Everywhere in Europe, for every independent worker there are twenty who work under an employer, and "wages" everywhere means what they usually amount to when the worker is one person and the owner of the capital that employs him is another.

What the ordinary wage works out to depends everywhere on the bargain usually struck between these two parties, whose interests are nowhere near the same. Workers want to get as much as they can; employers want to give as little as they can. Workers tend to band together to push wages up; employers band together to push them down.

It is not hard, though, to predict which side will normally win the dispute and force the other to accept its terms. Employers, being fewer, can combine far more easily. The law, moreover, either permits their combinations or at least does not ban them, while it does ban the workers'. There are no acts of Parliament against combining to lower the price of work, but plenty against combining to raise it. In any such dispute the employers can hold out far longer. A landlord, a farmer, a master manufacturer, or a merchant could generally live a year or two on the wealth they have already built up, even if they hired no one at all. Many workers could not last a week without work, few could last a month, and almost none a year. In the long run the worker may be as necessary to his employer as the employer is to him, but his need is far more immediate.

People say we rarely hear of employers combining, though we often hear of workers doing so. But anyone who concludes from this that employers seldom combine knows neither the world nor the subject. Employers are always and everywhere in a kind of tacit but constant and uniform agreement not to let wages rise above their present level. To break this agreement is everywhere a deeply unpopular act, and it brings a kind of disgrace on an employer among his neighbours and peers. We seldom hear of this combination precisely because it is the usual — one might say the natural — state of things, which nobody ever remarks on. Employers also sometimes form particular combinations to drive wages even below this level. These are always carried on with the utmost silence and secrecy until the moment they strike; and when the workers give in, as they sometimes do without a fight even though they feel it keenly, no one outside ever hears of it. Such combinations, however, are often met by a defensive combination of the workers, who sometimes also combine on their own, without any such provocation, simply to raise the price of their labour. Their stated reasons are sometimes the high price of food, sometimes the large profit their employers make from their work. But whether their combinations are offensive or defensive, we always hear plenty about them. To force a quick decision, they always resort to the loudest uproar, and sometimes to the most shocking violence and outrage. They are desperate, and they act with the recklessness of desperate men who must either starve or terrify their employers into giving in at once. The employers, on these occasions, are just as loud on their side, forever crying out for the help of the civil authorities and for the strict enforcement of the laws passed with such severity against the combination of servants, labourers, and journeymen. So the workers very rarely gain anything from the violence of these uproarious combinations, which — partly through the intervention of the authorities, partly through the greater staying power of the employers, partly through the need most of the workers are under to give in for the sake of immediate survival — generally end in nothing but the punishment or ruin of the ringleaders.

But although employers generally hold the advantage in disputes with their workers, there is nonetheless a certain level below which it seems impossible to push the ordinary wage even of the lowest kind of labour for any length of time.

A man has to live by his work, so his wages must at least be enough to keep him alive. In most cases they must be somewhat more, or he could never raise a family, and that kind of worker would die out after a single generation. On this reasoning Mr Cantillon seems to assume that the lowest sort of common labourer must everywhere earn at least double his own upkeep, so that on average he can raise two children — the wife's labour being taken as no more than enough to support herself, given that she must care for the children. But of the children born, it is reckoned, half die before reaching adulthood. So, by this account, the poorest labourers must on average try to raise at least four children, so that two have a fair chance of living that long. And the necessary upkeep of four children is supposed to come to roughly that of one grown man. The same author adds that the labour of an able-bodied slave is reckoned worth double his upkeep, and that the labour of the meanest worker, he thinks, cannot be worth less than that of an able-bodied slave. This much at least seems certain: to raise a family, the labour of husband and wife together, even in the lowest kind of common labour, must earn something more than is strictly needed for their own upkeep. But in what proportion — whether the one just mentioned, or some other — I will not undertake to decide.

There are certain circumstances, however, that sometimes give workers the upper hand and let them push their wages well above this rate, which is plainly the lowest level consistent with basic humanity.

When the demand in a country for those who live on wages — labourers, journeymen, servants of every kind — keeps rising; when each year provides work for more people than the year before, then workers have no need to combine to raise their wages. The shortage of hands sets off competition among employers, who bid against one another to get workers, and so break of their own accord through the natural agreement among employers not to raise wages. The demand for those who live on wages can clearly rise only in proportion to the rise in the funds set aside for paying wages. These funds are of two kinds: first, the revenue left over after upkeep; and second, the capital left over after what is needed to keep their employers' own businesses running.

When a landlord, an annuitant, or a man of money has a larger income than he thinks he needs to support his own family, he uses all or part of the surplus to keep one or more household servants. Increase that surplus, and he will naturally take on more such servants.

When an independent worker — a weaver or shoemaker, say — has more capital than he needs to buy his own materials and support himself until he can sell the work, he naturally uses the surplus to employ one or more journeymen so as to make a profit on their work. Increase that surplus, and he will naturally take on more journeymen.

So the demand for those who live on wages necessarily rises as a country's revenue and capital rise, and cannot possibly rise without them. The growth of revenue and capital is the growth of national wealth. The demand for those who live on wages therefore naturally rises with the growth of national wealth, and cannot possibly rise without it.

It is not the sheer size of a nation's wealth but its continual growth that drives wages up. Accordingly, the highest wages are found not in the richest countries but in the most thriving ones — those growing rich the fastest. England today is certainly a much richer country than any part of North America. Yet wages are much higher in North America than anywhere in England. In the province of New York in 1773, before the recent troubles began, common labourers earned three shillings and sixpence in local currency, equal to two shillings sterling, a day; ship-carpenters earned ten shillings and sixpence currency plus a pint of rum worth sixpence sterling, equal in all to six shillings and sixpence sterling; house-carpenters and bricklayers earned eight shillings currency, equal to four shillings and sixpence sterling; journeymen tailors earned five shillings currency, about two shillings and tenpence sterling. All these are above the London rate, and wages are said to be as high in the other colonies as in New York. Food is everywhere far cheaper in North America than in England. A famine has never been known there. Even in the worst seasons they have always had enough for themselves, though less to export. So if the money price of labour is higher there than anywhere in the mother country, its real price — the real command over the necessities and comforts of life that it gives the worker — must be higher by an even larger margin.

Though North America is not yet as rich as England, it is far more thriving, and is gaining wealth far more rapidly. The surest sign of a country's prosperity is a rise in its population. In Great Britain and most other European countries, the population is reckoned not to double in less than five hundred years. In the British colonies of North America, it has been found to double in twenty or twenty-five years. And in our own time this increase comes mainly not from the steady arrival of new settlers but from the rapid growth of the people themselves. Those who live to old age, it is said, often see fifty to a hundred descendants of their own body there, and sometimes many more. Labour is so well rewarded that a large family of children, far from being a burden, is a source of wealth and prosperity to the parents. The labour of each child, before it leaves home, is reckoned to be worth a clear hundred pounds' gain to them. A young widow with four or five small children — who among the middling or lower ranks in Europe would have little hope of a second husband — is there often courted as a kind of fortune. The value of children is the greatest of all spurs to marriage. No wonder, then, that people in North America generally marry very young. Despite the large increase such early marriages bring, there is a constant complaint of a shortage of hands in North America. It seems the demand for labourers, and the funds set aside to maintain them, grows even faster than labourers can be found to fill the jobs.

Even if a country's wealth is very great, you should not expect wages to be high there if that wealth has long stood still. The funds set aside for paying wages — the revenue and capital of its people — may be enormous; but if they have stayed at the same, or nearly the same, level for several centuries, the number of workers employed each year could easily supply, and even more than supply, the number needed the next year. There would seldom be any shortage of hands, and employers would not be forced to bid against one another to get them. Instead the workers would multiply beyond the available work. There would be a constant shortage of jobs, and the workers would have to bid against one another to get them. If in such a country wages had ever been more than enough to keep the worker alive and let him raise a family, the competition among workers and the self-interest of the employers would soon drive them down to the lowest rate consistent with basic humanity. China has long been one of the richest — that is, one of the most fertile, best cultivated, most industrious, and most populous — countries in the world. Yet it seems to have been at a standstill for a long time. Marco Polo, who visited it more than five hundred years ago, describes its farming, industry, and population in almost the same terms travellers use today. Perhaps even long before his time it had reached the full measure of wealth that its laws and institutions allow. Travellers' accounts, which disagree on much else, all agree on the low wages of labour and on how hard a worker there finds it to raise a family. If by digging the ground all day he can earn enough to buy a little rice that evening, he is content. The lot of craftsmen is, if anything, worse still. Instead of waiting idly in their workshops for customers to call, as in Europe, they roam the streets with the tools of their trade, offering their services and all but begging for work. The poverty of the lower ranks in China far exceeds that of the most wretched nations in Europe. Near Canton, it is commonly said, many hundreds — many thousands — of families have no home on land but live always in little fishing boats on the rivers and canals. The food they find there is so scanty that they eagerly scoop up the foulest garbage thrown overboard from any European ship. Any carrion — the carcass of a dead dog or cat, say — even half-rotten and stinking, is as welcome to them as the most wholesome food is to people elsewhere. Marriage is encouraged in China not by the profit of children but by the freedom to destroy them. In all the great towns, several are abandoned in the street every night, or drowned like puppies in the water. The carrying out of this horrid task is even said to be the openly acknowledged trade by which some people make their living.

China, however, though it may stand still, does not seem to be going backwards. Its towns are nowhere abandoned by their people. Land once cultivated is nowhere left neglected. So the same, or very nearly the same, amount of work must still be done each year, and the funds set aside to support it cannot have shrunk noticeably. The lowest class of labourers, then, despite their meagre subsistence, must somehow manage to keep their race going at its usual numbers.

It would be different, though, in a country where the funds set aside to support labour were noticeably shrinking. Each year the demand for servants and labourers, across all classes of work, would be less than it had been the year before. Many who had been raised to a higher class of work, unable to find a place in their own line, would gladly seek it in the lowest. That lowest class, already overcrowded with its own workers and now flooded by the overflow from all the others, would face such fierce competition for jobs that wages there would fall to the most wretched and scanty subsistence. Many would not find work even on these harsh terms, and would either starve or be driven to scrape a living by begging or by committing perhaps the worst of crimes. Want, famine, and death would at once take hold in that class and spread upward to all the higher ones, until the country's population was cut down to what the surviving revenue and capital — whatever had escaped the tyranny or disaster that destroyed the rest — could comfortably support. This is perhaps roughly the present state of Bengal and some other English settlements in the East Indies. In a fertile country that had already lost much of its population, where food should therefore not be very hard to come by, and where nonetheless three or four hundred thousand people die of hunger in a single year, we can be sure that the funds set aside to support the labouring poor are fast decaying. The difference between the spirit of the British constitution, which protects and governs North America, and that of the trading company that oppresses and lords it over the East Indies could hardly be better shown than by the contrasting condition of those two regions.

Generous pay for labour, then, is both the necessary effect and the natural symptom of growing national wealth. The bare subsistence of the labouring poor, on the other hand, is the natural sign that things have stalled, and their starving condition the sign that they are sliding fast backwards.

In Great Britain today, wages plainly seem to be more than just enough to let a worker raise a family. To convince ourselves of this, we need not go into any tedious or uncertain calculation of the lowest sum on which it could be done. There are many plain signs that wages in this country are nowhere set by that lowest rate consistent with basic humanity.

First, almost everywhere in Great Britain there is a difference, even in the lowest kind of labour, between summer and winter wages. Summer wages are always higher. But because of the extra cost of fuel, supporting a family is most expensive in winter. So since wages are highest when this expense is lowest, it is clear they are not set by what the expense requires but by the amount and presumed value of the work. It might be objected that a worker ought to save part of his summer wages to cover his winter costs, so that over the whole year his wages come to no more than is needed to keep his family through the whole year. But a slave, or anyone wholly dependent on us for his immediate survival, would not be treated this way. His daily upkeep would be matched to his daily needs.

Second, wages in Great Britain do not move with the price of food. Food prices vary everywhere from year to year, often from month to month. Yet in many places the money price of labour stays the same, sometimes for half a century at a stretch. So if in these places the labouring poor can support their families in expensive years, they must be comfortable in years of moderate plenty and well-off in years of unusual cheapness. The high food prices of the past ten years have not, in many parts of the kingdom, been matched by any noticeable rise in the money price of labour. In some parts they have — owing probably more to a rise in the demand for labour than to the rise in food prices.

Third, just as food prices vary more from year to year than wages do, so wages vary more from place to place than food prices do. The prices of bread and butcher's meat are generally the same, or nearly so, throughout most of the United Kingdom. These, and most other goods sold by retail — the way the labouring poor buy everything — are generally just as cheap, or cheaper, in large towns than in remote parts of the country, for reasons I will explain later. But wages in a large town and its surroundings are often a fourth or a fifth — twenty or twenty-five per cent — higher than a few miles away. Eighteen pence a day may be reckoned the usual rate in and around London. A few miles off it drops to fourteen or fifteen pence. Tenpence may be reckoned the rate in and around Edinburgh. A few miles off it drops to eightpence, the usual rate for common labour across most of the Lowlands of Scotland, where it varies a good deal less than in England. Such a gap in prices, which it seems is not always enough to move a man from one parish to another, would necessarily prompt the shipping of the bulkiest goods not only from parish to parish but from one end of the kingdom — almost from one end of the world — to the other, until the gap was nearly levelled out. For all that has been said about human flightiness and inconstancy, experience plainly shows that of all kinds of cargo, man is the hardest to transport. So if the labouring poor can support their families in the parts of the kingdom where wages are lowest, they must be well-off where wages are highest.
Fourth, the swings in the price of labour not only fail to match those in the price of food, in place or in time, but are often the exact opposite.

Grain, the food of the common people, is dearer in Scotland than in England, from which Scotland receives very large supplies almost every year. But English corn must sell dearer in Scotland, where it is brought, than in England, where it comes from; and, relative to its quality, it cannot sell dearer in Scotland than the Scotch corn competing with it in the same market. Grain quality depends mainly on how much flour or meal it yields at the mill, and in this respect English grain is so far superior to Scotch that, though it often looks dearer by bulk, it is generally cheaper in reality — relative to its quality, or even by weight. The price of labour, by contrast, is dearer in England than in Scotland. So if the labouring poor can support their families in one part of the United Kingdom, they must be well-off in the other. Oatmeal, it is true, supplies the common people in Scotland with the greatest and best part of their food, which is generally far inferior to that of their counterparts of the same rank in England. But this difference in diet is the effect, not the cause, of the difference in wages — though by a strange misunderstanding I have often heard it given as the cause. It is not because one man keeps a carriage while his neighbour goes on foot that the first is rich and the second poor; rather, the first is rich and so keeps a carriage, and the second is poor and so walks.

Over the course of the last century, taking one year with another, grain was dearer in both parts of the United Kingdom than during the present one. This is a fact that can no longer be reasonably doubted, and the proof is, if anything, even more decisive for Scotland than for England. In Scotland it rests on the public fiars — annual valuations, made on oath according to the actual state of the markets, of every sort of grain in every county of Scotland. If such direct proof needed any backing, I would add that the same has held in France, and probably in most of Europe. For France the proof is perfectly clear. But while it is certain that in both parts of the United Kingdom grain was somewhat dearer in the last century than now, it is equally certain that labour was much cheaper. So if the labouring poor could raise their families then, they must be much more comfortable now. In the last century the most usual day-wages for common labour across most of Scotland were sixpence in summer and fivepence in winter. Three shillings a week — very nearly the same rate — is still paid in parts of the Highlands and Western Isles. Across most of the Lowlands the most usual wage for common labour is now eightpence a day; tenpence, sometimes a shilling, around Edinburgh, in the counties bordering England — probably because of that nearness — and in a few other places where the demand for labour has lately risen considerably, around Glasgow, Carron, Ayrshire, and so on. In England, improvements in farming, manufacturing, and trade began much earlier than in Scotland. The demand for labour, and hence its price, must have risen with them. So in the last century as in the present, wages were higher in England than in Scotland. They have also risen considerably since then, though, because of the greater variety of rates paid in different places, it is harder to say by how much. In 1614 a foot soldier's pay was the same as today, eightpence a day. When the rate was first set, it would naturally have been pegged to the usual wage of common labourers, the class from which foot soldiers are usually drawn. Lord Chief Justice Hales, writing in the reign of Charles II, reckons the necessary cost of a labourer's family of six — father, mother, two children able to do something, and two who cannot — at ten shillings a week, or twenty-six pounds a year. If they cannot earn this by their labour, he supposes, they must make it up by begging or stealing. He seems to have looked into the matter very carefully. (See his scheme for the maintenance of the poor in Burn's History of the Poor Laws.) In 1688 Mr Gregory King, whose skill in political arithmetic Dr Davenant praises so highly, reckoned the ordinary income of labourers and out-servants at fifteen pounds a year per family, which he took to consist on average of three and a half persons. So his figure, though it looks different, comes very nearly to the same thing at bottom as Judge Hales's. Both put the weekly cost of such families at about twentypence a head. Both the cash income and the cash expense of such families have risen considerably since then through most of the kingdom — more in some places, less in others — though perhaps almost nowhere as much as some exaggerated accounts of present wages have lately led the public to believe. It must be noted that the price of labour can nowhere be pinned down very precisely, since different rates are often paid in the same place for the same kind of work, not only according to the worker's differing skill but according to the easiness or harshness of the employer. Where wages are not fixed by law, all we can claim to determine is what the most usual rates are; and experience seems to show that the law can never set them properly, however often it has pretended to.

The real reward of labour — the real quantity of necessities and comforts of life it can buy the worker — has, over the present century, risen by perhaps an even larger margin than its money price. Not only has grain grown somewhat cheaper, but many other things that give the industrious poor a pleasant and wholesome variety in their diet have grown a great deal cheaper. Potatoes, for example, now cost across most of the kingdom less than half what they did thirty or forty years ago. The same can be said of turnips, carrots, and cabbages — things once grown only with the spade but now commonly raised by the plough. All sorts of garden produce, too, have grown cheaper. Most of the apples, and even of the onions, eaten in Great Britain were in the last century imported from Flanders. The great improvements in the coarser branches of linen and woollen manufacture give workers cheaper and better clothing, and those in the manufacture of the coarser metals give them cheaper and better tools of trade as well as many handy and pleasant pieces of household furniture. Soap, salt, candles, leather, and fermented drinks have, it is true, grown a good deal dearer, chiefly because of the taxes laid on them. But the amount of these that the labouring poor are obliged to use is so small that the rise in their price does not offset the fall in that of so many other things. The common complaint that luxury now reaches even the lowest ranks, and that the labouring poor will no longer be content with the food, clothing, and lodging that once satisfied them, may convince us that it is not just the money price of labour that has risen, but its real reward.

Is this improvement in the condition of the lower ranks to be counted as good for society, or as a drawback? The answer seems at first perfectly plain. Servants, labourers, and workers of various kinds make up by far the largest part of every great society. And whatever improves the condition of the greater part can never count as a drawback to the whole. No society can surely be flourishing and happy when by far the greater part of its members are poor and miserable. It is only fair, besides, that those who feed, clothe, and house the whole body of the people should have a large enough share of the product of their own labour to be themselves tolerably well fed, clothed, and housed.

Poverty, though it certainly discourages marriage, does not always prevent it. It even seems to favour having children. A half-starved Highland woman often bears more than twenty children, while a pampered fine lady is often unable to bear any, and is generally worn out by two or three. Barrenness, so common among women of fashion, is very rare among those of lower station. Luxury, in women, while it may inflame the appetite for pleasure, always seems to weaken, and often to destroy altogether, the capacity to bear children.

But poverty, though it does not prevent children from being born, is extremely unfavourable to raising them. The tender plant comes up, but in such cold soil and such a harsh climate it soon withers and dies. In the Scottish Highlands, I have often been told, it is not uncommon for a mother who has borne twenty children to have only two alive. Several officers of great experience have assured me that, far from replenishing their regiment, they have never been able to keep it supplied even with drummers and fifers from all the soldiers' children born in it. Yet a finer crop of children is seldom seen anywhere than around a barracks. Very few of them, it seems, reach the age of thirteen or fourteen. In some places half the children die before they are four, in many before they are seven, and almost everywhere before they are nine or ten. This heavy mortality, however, is found everywhere mainly among the children of the common people, who cannot afford to tend them with the same care as those of better station. Though their marriages are generally more fruitful than those of the fashionable, a smaller share of their children reach maturity. In foundling hospitals, and among children raised on parish charity, the mortality is greater still than among the common people's.

Every species of animal naturally multiplies in proportion to its means of subsistence, and none can ever multiply beyond it. But in a civilized society it is only among the lower ranks that scarcity of subsistence can set limits to the further multiplication of the human race — and it can do so in no other way than by destroying a great part of the children that their fruitful marriages produce.

Generous pay for labour, by letting the poor provide better for their children and so raise more of them, naturally tends to widen those limits. It is worth noting, too, that it necessarily does this as nearly as possible in the proportion that the demand for labour requires. If demand keeps rising, the reward of labour must necessarily encourage the marriage and multiplication of workers in just such a way that a continually growing population can supply that continually growing demand. If the reward ever falls below what this requires, the shortage of hands soon raises it; and if it ever rises above it, the excessive multiplication of workers soon brings it back down to the needed rate. The market would be so understocked with labour in the one case, and so overstocked in the other, that the price would soon be forced back to the proper rate that the society's circumstances required. In this way the demand for people, like the demand for any other commodity, necessarily governs the production of people — speeding it up when it goes too slowly and slowing it down when it goes too fast. It is this demand that regulates and settles the rate of reproduction in every country of the world: making it rapidly rising in North America, slow and gradual in Europe, and altogether stationary in China.

The upkeep of a slave, it has been said, falls on his master, while that of a free servant falls on himself. Yet in reality the upkeep of the free servant is just as much at his master's expense as that of the slave. The wages paid to journeymen and servants of every kind must be enough to keep the race of journeymen and servants going, according to whether the society's demand happens to be rising, falling, or stationary. But though the upkeep of a free servant equally falls on his master, it generally costs him much less than that of a slave. The fund set aside for replacing or repairing, so to speak, a slave's wear and tear is usually managed by a careless master or a negligent overseer.
